articles.title_orig: Project B picks China as first stop for new women's basketball tour
articles.title_zh: Project B picks China as first stop for new women's basketball tour
articles.content_orig:
Project B is going to China in 2027, the women's basketball league announced on Wednesday, Sept. 30.
Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang province, will the first stop on the Project B's inaugural circuit. The league plans to play at the Hangzhou Olympic Sports AT Center Gymnasium from Jan. 19–24. The league announced the news with help from co-founder and chief strategy officer Russell Westbrook, co-founder and chief basketball officer Alana Beard and Chinese basketball player Li Meng.
“China has always had incredible energy around basketball, and I’ve experienced that personally throughout my career,” Westbrook said via release. “Project B is connecting basketball with culture in each place we play. I have deep respect for the history and tradition here, and also the constant drive to create what comes next. This combination is powerful.”
Training camp and Project B's first draft will be in Seoul from Jan. 6-12 ahead of players arriving in Hangzhou. The league's first season will then begin the following week. Additional details about the Hangzhou stop are expected to be announced at a later date.
“From a basketball perspective, we wanted our first stop to set the standard,” Beard said. “We’re bringing the best players in the world together to compete at the highest level, and we’re also creating an environment where they can experience new cultures and build real connections with fans. Starting in Hangzhou gives us an incredible stage for both.”
Project B's women's basketball league has more than 20 WNBA players who have signed on, including Azzi Fudd and Alanna Smith of the Dallas Wings, Alyssa Thomas of the Mercury, Awa Fam of the Seattle Storm, Jewell Loyd of the Las Vegas Aces, Jonquel Jones of the New York Liberty, Kamilla Cardoso of the Chicago Sky, Kelsey Mitchell and Sophie Cunningham of the Fever and Nneka Ogwumike , who retired from the WNBA at the end of the season.
The concept for Project B is to have two separate leagues ― men and women ― with six teams, each with 11 players. Those teams will compete in a global circuit slated to kick off in Jan. 2027 and run through April 2027. Each city will host a 10-day event, crowning a city champion, and those victories will count towards a season-long championship. Project B has revealed that, outside of Hangzhou, it will also play in Tokyo, Japan and Valencia, Spain.
Athletes who play in Project B are expected to have equity in the league. Project B hasn’t disclosed any salaries yet, but a league spokesperson previously told USA TODAY Sports they are “higher than anything you’ve ever seen in women’s sports."
The global basketball league has multiple investors, including women’s basketball legends Cheryl Miller, Candace Parker and Lauren Jackson and NFL Hall of Fame quarterback Steve Young. Additionally, Project B has secured Host Broadcast Services (HBS) to be the official broadcaster for the league’s inaugural circuit . HBS has broadcast the FIFA World Cup since 2002. The games will stream live on YouTube.

articles.title_orig: Passengers overcame co-pilot who tried to crash flydubai flight, Netanyahu says
articles.title_zh: Passengers overcame co-pilot who tried to crash flydubai flight, Netanyahu says
articles.content_orig:
Israeli officials investigating if incident, which forced plane to make emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, was attempted terror attack
One of the pilots of a plane flying from the UAE to Israel stabbed his co-pilot and appeared to try to crash the plane, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said, as Israeli officials said they were investigating if the incident was an attempted terror attack on Israelis.
The plane was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after the apparent attack, with the two pilots wounded but other passengers safe, according to a statement by Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz international airport, more commonly known as Tabuk airport.
The pilot accused of carrying out the attack was currently being questioned by Saudi authorities, Netanyahu said.
The Israeli defence minister, Israel Katz, described the incident as an “attempted jihadist attack”. “The terrorist had a single objective: to crash the plane, killing everyone onboard,” Katz said, adding that the attack was stopped due to the “heroism of several passengers”.
Israeli officials, speaking on condition of anonymity to reporters, said the attacker was an Omani national and that Israel’s current assessment of the incident was that it was a terror attack. There was no comment on the attack from either Oman or the United Arab Emirates.
Two and a half hours after taking off from Dubai, the plane sent out an emergency signal – squawk code 7700, indicating a general emergency – before sending out another – code 7500, indicating a potential hijacking attempt.
The plane also abruptly descended, falling about 17,000 ft in a two-minute span, before diverting from Jordanian airspace towards Tabuk airport, in north-western Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely. Israeli officials told Reuters that the cabin crew took control of the cockpit and helped land the plane after the attack.
Videos of the incident showed passengers screaming as the plane descended, as well as a blood-covered man who appeared to be the pilot injured and on the floor.
“The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane,” passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon told reporters via her mother’s phone at Tel Aviv airport.
“It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him,” she said, adding that a doctor on board treated the wounded pilot.
Israeli officials’ initially scrambled fighter jets after the emergency signals were sent out, fearing an attack on Israel or that the plane would be diverted to a third country. A spokesperson for the Israeli prime minister’s office then said the incident was not a hijacking, as media reports circulated of a fight between the two pilots.
As more information emerged about the violent nature of the attack, Israeli and international media began to report officials anonymously saying an investigation had been opened into whether this was an attack on Israelis.
Israeli authorities have so far refrained from publicly calling the alleged attack a suspected terror incident, besides the far-right national security minister. Itamar Ben-Gvir. Ben-Gvir said on X that “terrorism is a devil with whom no agreement must be reached”, referring to the incident.
The head of the Israeli military, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, postponed his planned visit to the US next week over the incident, where he was meant to have a meeting with US joint chiefs of staff and the head of US Central Command.
The circumstances of the brawl between the pilots were unclear, with passengers recounting confusing moments and blood being spilt.
Yasmin Abu Kaiss, whose daughter was on the flight, told Reuters her daughter said she had heard screaming and a man with a knife had put a pilot on the floor, and that there was blood everywhere.
Pictures published by Israeli media showed a passenger wearing a blood-soaked shirt. The Guardian could not independently verify the image.
The incident came just days after the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, warned there were indications an attack would be carried out during Israel’s October elections. The Israeli military, quoted by Israeli media, said it had no intelligence that an attack was being planned on Israel.
Yair Lapid, an opposition figure and former prime minister, cast doubt on the connection between the alleged attack and Netanyahu’s warning, saying that a security briefing on Tuesday night gave no information about a possible incident similar to what happened on Wednesday.
Israel experienced a series of hijackings and attacks on planes by Palestinian militants in the 1960s and 1970s, but has not had anything similar in decades. The country maintains some of the strictest airport security procedures in the world, including security checks before passengers board Israel-bound flights.
Flights between Dubai and Israel started after the countries normalised ties in 2020. Israel does not have diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, but in 2025 landed a plane in Riyadh because of a medical emergency.
Flydubai confirmed that flight FZ 1073 en route to Ben Gurion experienced an incident and landed safely in Tabuk on Wednesday. “Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities,” the carrier said. “Further updates will be issued as additional confirmed details become available.”
Israeli media reported that a later flydubai flight heading to Tel Aviv turned around in mid-air back towards Dubai after the incident.

articles.title_orig: Actor Chad Lowe's daughter Fiona Lowe dies at 13
articles.title_zh: Actor Chad Lowe's daughter Fiona Lowe dies at 13
articles.content_orig:
US actor Chad Lowe and his wife, producer Kim Painter, have said they are "deeply heartbroken" following the death of their "beloved" 13-year-old daughter Fiona.
"She was a loving young girl who was smart, creative and loved to dance," the family said in a statement to Page Six , external and People , external .
"She was adored by her sisters and she was deeply loved by her parents. In fact, she was the light of our lives.
"Her passing is devastating for our entire family and we ask for prayers and privacy at this time."
The statement concluded: "If you or someone you know is struggling with mental health, please reach out to the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988."
Chad Lowe, the brother of fellow actor Rob Lowe, won an Emmy Award in 1993 for TV show Life Goes On and has appeared in other programmes including Pretty Little Liars and Supergirl.
He and Painter are also parents to daughters Mabel, 17, and Nixie, 10.
Information about organisations that provide support in the UK is available on the BBC Action Line website .

articles.title_orig: Tennessee execution of lone woman on death row halted by federal appeals court
articles.title_zh: Tennessee execution of lone woman on death row halted by federal appeals court
articles.content_orig:
A federal appeals court Wednesday morning halted the execution of the lone woman on Tennessee’s death row about an hour before it was scheduled to be carried out.
In a last-minute decision, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth District said it needed to review claims that Christa Pike’s legal team made in a bid to stop her execution. At issue is whether Pike can reopen a court proceeding centered around her allegations that she was sexually abused beginning when she was a child, which the state acknowledged at a special hearing in August.
“The interests of justice and the finality of Pike’s impending execution compel the entry of a short stay of execution in order to properly analyze the parties’ fully briefed arguments and resolve the issues on the merits,” the court said.
It’s unclear how long the execution may be halted. It was scheduled for 10 a.m. local time in Nashville.
“The court has stayed this, recognizing the serious concerns about Christa’s scheduled execution,” said Stephen Ferrell of the Federal Defenders Services of Eastern Tennessee.
Both Gov. Bill Lee and the Supreme Court had said they would not stop Pike’s execution.
Before learning Monday that Lee would not be intervening in her case, Pike, 50, wrote in a letter to NBC News, shared by her spiritual adviser: “Whether my clemency is granted or not, I am at peace.”
“I am not afraid to die,” wrote Pike, who has been on death row for more than three decades. “I’m only nervous about the process.”
If executed, Pike would be the first woman in more than 200 years that the state puts to death, according to historical records .
In 1995, Pike was 18 when Knoxville police say she and two teenage accomplices worked together to torture, slash and fatally beat Colleen Slemmer, 19. Police say Pike and the others lured Slemmer, a classmate in their Job Corps training program, to an abandoned steam plant at the nearby University of Tennessee and attacked her.
The case became sensationalized when investigators said it was tied to the occult because someone had carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest and Pike bragged to another student that she had kept a fragment of the victim’s skull as a “souvenir.”
Pike doesn’t dispute her role in the grisly killing. But details about her upbringing, marked by years of sexual and physical abuse and neglect, were not shared with the jury that sentenced her to death. Her lawyers believe that if such evidence of abuse were presented at a trial now, a death sentence would not be guaranteed.
They had asked the Supreme Court to halt Pike’s execution, saying that she suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder stemming from being molested and raped beginning when she was a toddler. Being held down and strapped to a gurney, they wrote, will likely create “severe mental suffering and superadded psychological terror under Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol.”
The state hasn’t denied that Pike has suffered from abuse. But in a response filed Monday, the attorney general’s office said a judge already concluded last month that it was “speculative whether Pike would suffer” greater mental harm from how the lethal injection protocol is carried out.
The Supreme Court appeared to be Pike’s remaining chance for a reprieve after Lee said he was upholding her death sentence “after deliberate consideration.” The high court denied her petition Tuesday evening.
Pike’s lawyers said Monday they were “saddened and heartbroken” that the governor would not be granting clemency.
Another woman, Gaile Owens , was on Tennessee’s death row with Pike until 2010, when Gov. Phil Bredesen changed her sentence to life in prison.
In her letter, Pike wrote that people have seen a “limited public persona that has been the only narrative” about her. Her lawyers had tried to convince Lee that she was a product of a tumultuous childhood.
“Stepping into the chaos of Christa’s life that led her to that moment will not justify her actions that night,” one of her lawyers, Randall Spivey, said of when she committed her crime. “But the chaos will show you that Christa was broken, not evil.”
Pike’s lawyers also point to her age and how it led to such a different outcome in her case.
While she faced a death sentence because of her first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder conviction in Slemmer’s death, another conspirator was spared: Pike’s boyfriend, who was 17 at the time. Tadaryl Shipp received a life sentence because he was a juvenile and remains eligible for parole. Shipp testified at his post-conviction hearing that he was the one who carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest.
The third accomplice — Shadolla Peterson, then 18 — served as a lookout in the crime and received probation in exchange for her cooperation.
Pike told police she “wasn’t even thinking” when she assaulted Slemmer and that she had been jealous believing the victim was trying to steal Shipp’s attention. Pike’s lawyers say that her age would have been more of a factor today, given how scientific research has evolved in understanding that young people’s brains are still developing well beyond their teen years.
In addition, her lawyers say that her legal representatives at the time could have accepted a deal from prosecutors who were offering a life sentence without parole in return for a guilty plea.
Pike sobbed as the judge told her she would die by electrocution, then the only form of execution in Tennessee before the state moved to lethal injection as its primary method.
She pleaded through tears : “Can I please hug my mom?”
Pike entered prison, where she was placed into solitary confinement for up to 23 hours a day and prescribed Prozac to treat her obsessive-compulsive disorder. Early on, she struggled to express remorse.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in her clemency petition.
Three years ago, Bethany Brand, a psychologist specializing in trauma, was asked by Pike’s lawyers to assess whether she suffers from psychological disorders and consider if any contributed to the crime.
She sat with Pike at her Nashville prison and reviewed police reports, past medical examinations and other files in her case detailing physical and sexual abuse. Brand learned that Pike’s parents were not stable figures in her life. Her mother’s boyfriends and other men had molested her from a young age, the files said. She did poorly in school, living with other family members in West Virginia and North Carolina. At 17 — one year before she would take part in Slemmer’s murder — Pike reported to North Carolina police that she was walking to the store when a man threw her to the ground and raped her. No one was ever arrested.
In her final report, Brand wrote that the adults in Pike’s life failed her. Doctors only diagnosed a bipolar disorder a few years after she was already in prison.
The level of trauma Pike was subjected to “is almost impossible to grasp because it is so severe,” Brand wrote.
She told NBC News that medications in prison have helped Pike tremendously and that she now has “empathy and great regret” for what she did. But, she added, Pike’s case is a lesson of the need for greater awareness surrounding women’s mental health and recognizing trauma and untreated mental illness.
“In Christa’s case, nobody was trying to get her help,” Brand said.

Martinez recalled how, after the investigation ended, she did not realize all of her daughter’s body parts weren’t buried with her remains, as some had been retained as trial evidence. She had to pick up Slemmer’s skull from the courthouse, and remembers that the medical examiner’s office mailed her other parts later. Iraqi armed factions backed by Tehran said Wednesday they were "not bound by any timeline or agreement" to surrender their weapons to the state, as the government seeks to disarm them under mounting U.S. pressure.
A military spokesman for Kataeb Hezbollah, Jaafar al-Husseini, said at an event to celebrate the withdrawal of U.S.-led coalition forces that the factions had been in talks on "regulating" their weapons but "have not yet received a response from the Iraqi government."
"Based on this, the Islamic Resistance declares that it is not bound by any timetable or agreement that any governmental or political party has spoken of or may speak of," al-Husseini said.
The U.S. military announced on Wednesday it had officially pulled out of Iraq after 12 years fighting the Islamic State. The U.S. and Iraqi government had agreed to a pullout by Sept. 30 and began the process over recent months.
The militias in Iraq have launched attacks on other Gulf countries in the wake of the U.S. and Israeli launching war on Iran in February. The U.S. and Saudi Arabia launched joint strikes on those militias in late July.
A British maritime agency said Wednesday that unknown projectiles struck three ships in the Strait of Hormuz the previous day. A crude oil tanker and two other vessels had each "been struck by an unknown projectile," the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center (UKMTO) said.
It had earlier described one of the vessels as an LNG tanker, before later describing it as a tanker.
The Strait of Hormuz is at the center of the war between Iran and the United States.
Around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas passed through the strategic shipping lane before the war. But since the conflict broke out, Tehran has been attempting to block the passage of commercial ships, firing on vessels it accuses of unauthorized crossings.
Washington has responded with a counterblockade of Iranian ports in an effort to prevent Tehran from exporting its oil.
An Iranian woman sentenced to death over protests earlier this year has begged the international community to save her life and those of others facing the death penalty, according to an audio message she sent from prison that was shared Wednesday by rights groups.
The plea by Mahboubeh Shahbani, 33, from a prison in the eastern Iranian city of Mashhad, came after authorities executed two more men on charges linked to the major anti-regime protests in January.
Rights groups accuse Iran of ramping up executions of high-profile prisoners in a bid to intimidate the population and ensure there is no repeat of the protests, which preceded the U.S. and Israel launching their joint war against the Islamic republic on Feb. 28.
Iran more than doubled its use of executions in 2025 , Amnesty International said earlier this year.
"The sentence handed down to me shows that many others are in danger of execution," Shahbani said in a telephone call from the phone for prisoners in Mashhad's Vakilabad prison.
"I am not worried about myself. I am worried for the others whose sentences have been upheld," she said in the call, an audio recording of which was shared by Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHR) and the U.S.-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).
It was not immediately possible to verify the authenticity of the message.
"I call on everyone - the public, the U.N., human rights organizations. Not just for me but for all the others whose sentences have been upheld and who have spent months sleeping in fear and stress at night," she said. "I call on them to do something."
According to the U.S.-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), Shahbani was convicted of carrying out actions "to strengthen Israel, the U.S., and individuals affiliated with opposition groups" in the protests.
IHR said she had merely used her motorcycle to transport injured protesters.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said lasting security in the Persian Gulf and its waterways depends primarily on cooperation among, and is the responsibility of regional countries, in a message marking World Maritime Day.
"The Strait of Hormuz, as one of the most important maritime passages, has a special position in the security and economy of the region and the world," Pezeshkian said, according to Iranian state news agency IRNA.
"Our approach to this strategic waterway is responsible and based on maintaining the security, stability and interests of the countries of the region," he said. "We believe that lasting security in the Persian Gulf and its waterways depends, more than anything else, on the cooperation, responsibility and role of the countries of the region."
Iran has repeatedly targeted U.S. regional allies around the Gulf since the war began in late February, as well as commercial vessels it accuses of attempting to navigate the Strait of Hormuz without its permission.
Iran's semi-official Fars news agency claimed Wednesday that Iranian security agencies had received intelligence suggesting Israeli plans to orchestrate a false-flag "mass-casualty incident" to blame on the Islamic Republic.
Fars, which is linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said intelligence obtained by an Iranian security agency pointed to a scenario it said had been proposed by the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad to the prime minister's office involving an operation against aircraft or airports in the region.
The report claimed the plan was to "create a mass-casualty incident and provide the grounds for attributing responsibility for it to Iran."
Fars reported separately on the FlyDubai incident Wednesday that saw a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv diverted for an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a violent cockpit altercation, which some reports suggested could have started as an attempted hijacking by one crewmember. The Iranian news agency did not link the FlyDubai incident to the purported intelligence about a possible Israeli false-flag operation.
A British maritime agency said that unknown projectiles struck three ships in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.
A crude oil tanker, LNG tanker and a third vessel had each "been struck by an unknown projectile", the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) said, without elaborating.

The U.S. military announced on Wednesday that it has completed the withdrawal of all American troops from Iraq, ending a 12-year mission to fight the Islamic State group.
The withdrawal, agreed on two years ago, comes against the backdrop of the ongoing war between the United States and Iran that has also sometimes spilled over into Iraq, with Iran-backed militias firing on U.S. troops and the U.S. striking the groups' strongholds.
The withdrawal was celebrated by Iran-backed groups but raised concerns among some other Iraqis, particularly in the Kurdish region.
"The expulsion of the occupation forces, defeated, from the land of Iraq is the beginning of full sovereignty," Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, a security official with the powerful Kataib Hezbollah militia, said in a statement.
U.S. troops pulled out of bases in most areas of Iraq last year but maintained a small presence of hundreds of troops in the semiautonomous northern Kurdish region. Iran-backed Iraqi militias also have coordinated with Yemen's Houthi rebels to attack Saudi Arabia.

articles.title_orig: Eli Lilly says closely watched combo obesity regimen boosts weight loss in mid-stage trial
articles.title_zh: Eli Lilly says closely watched combo obesity regimen boosts weight loss in mid-stage trial
articles.content_orig:
Eli Lilly on Wednesday said its experimental combination regimen showed greater weight loss than a high dose of its top-selling drug, tirzepatide, alone in a mid-stage trial on patients with obesity and Type 2 diabetes.
The combo therapy met the study's main goals in a population that typically struggles to lose weight. The results boost hopes that it could serve as an alternative blockbuster treatment option for people who didn't respond to or see the results they wanted on the current GLP-1 products on the market. Lilly said it plans to start Phase 3 trials on the regimen at the end of the year.
The combination treatment combines Lilly's experimental drug eloralintide, which targets amylin – a hormone in the pancreas involved in appetite and satiety – with a low dose of tirzepatide, the active ingredient in its obesity injection Zepbound and its diabetes counterpart Mounjaro.
Tirzepatide targets two gut hormones, GLP-1 and GIP. Lilly believes that hitting all three pathways, including amylin, can further reduce appetite and improve weight loss – and the combo drug did just that in the 48-week Phase 2 trial.
People taking the highest dose of the combo regimen lost up to 23.3% of their weight, or around 54 pounds, on average. That treatment combined 9 milligrams of the amylin drug and 15 milligrams of tirzepatide.
Meanwhile, patients taking only a 15-milligram dose of tirzepatide saw 14.8% weight loss, or 34.4 pounds, on average. Those who took eloralintide alone lost up to 12.3% of their weight, or 28.6 pounds, on average.
"Patients may not get what they need from a drug like tirzepatide," Ken Custer, president of Lilly Cardiometabolic Health, said in an interview. "They may not get what they need from a drug like a eloralintide on its own. The ability to combine them together and provide even greater weight loss – that's definitely one obvious" benefit of the new regimen.
The combo treatment also lowered a key measure of blood sugar levels – A1C – by up to 2.9% on average. Higher-dose tirzepatide reduced A1C by up to 2.4% on average, while the amylin drug lowered it by up to 1.4% on average.
Lilly may face more questions from investors and the medical community about how well patients tolerate and stay on the highly effective combination therapy.
More patients on the combo regimen – 10.8% to 27%, depending on the dose – discontinued treatment due to side effects compared to the 2.9% of people on tirzepatide alone in the trial.
Up to 10.8% of people on the amylin drug alone discontinued treatment due to side effects, compared to 16.7% with placebo.
Lilly said the side effects were more frequent in groups taking the combination regimen compared to tirzepatide or the amylin drug alone. The most common side effects of the combo therapy were gastrointestinal-related, generally mild or moderate in severity, and mainly occurred when patients increased doses in the trial.
But Custer cautioned against reading too much into the combo regimen's discontinuation rates in Phase 2. He noted that the highest dose of tirzepatide similarly showed elevated rates, around 25%, in a mid-stage trial back in 2018.
"It's probably not the best indicator of the tolerability of a medicine," Custer told CNBC. "We do things in Phase 1 and Phase 2 to test what the molecule can do from an efficacy perspective. We also learn from those studies about how we should administer them, and then we make changes. We do this every time."
Lilly plans to adjust the dosing regimens for the combo treatment in Phase 3 trials, "and we expect that we'll end up with a very favorable balance of efficacy and tolerability," Custer added.
Lilly is also planning to advance a co-formulation of the two drugs in Phase 3 trials, meaning that patients will only need to administer one injection with both tirzepatide and eloralintide.
Results were presented at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes in Milan, Italy. On Wednesday, Lilly said it plans to advance the combo product into Phase 3 studies by the end of 2026.
Ahead of the Phase 2 data, some analysts said the study positions Lilly's combination regimen as a direct comparison to Novo's next-generation obesity treatment CagriSema, which combines drugs targeting amylin and GLP-1.
Custer said the combination regimen could "turn out to be a really winning approach."
"This very physiological approach of combining GLP-1, GIP, and amylin, which are three nutrient-stimulated hormones that your body releases naturally in response to food and promotes satiety, putting those things together may just make for a drug that is broadly used," he said. "You're sort of lightly engaging three hormone systems rather than blasting any one of them."
Ahead of Lilly's data, Leerink Partners analyst David Risinger said he sees "mega-blockbuster" sales for Lilly's amylin-targeting drug, eloralintide, which is also being studied as a standalone treatment. He told CNBC the drug likely has "much greater market potential than the Street currently realized," noting that there are "millions" of patients who didn't see results from existing GLP-1 treatments or couldn't tolerate their side effects.

articles.content_orig:
By BRIAN VINER, FILM CRITIC
Published: 18:12 EDT, 29 September 2026 | Updated: 02:41 EDT, 30 September 2026
Rating: Four out of five stars
At the end of last week's world premiere of Digger – which was also the Royal Film Performance – many of us headed for the exits so perplexed by what we'd just seen that it didn't seem especially odd, when we got there, to find that we weren't allowed to leave the cinema.
Digger is so bizarre that I wasn't alone in wondering whether we were all caught up in a brazen piece of performance art, barricaded into the Odeon Leicester Square as an unwitting part of the narrative.
In fact, the explanation was more prosaic. We just had to wait until the Prince and Princess of Wales had safely departed, along with their entourage.
But you get the picture. Alejandro G Inarritu's darkly comic satire leaves the imagination reeling.
The title character, a super-rich Texan oil tycoon, is played by Tom Cruise, barely recognisable under prosthetics that subvert Hollywood norms.
Grey, jowly, balding and pot-bellied, 64-year-old Cruise as Digger Rockwell, ruthlessly acquisitive boss of Rockwell Oil, at long last looks his age.
I've already seen Digger twice...this is bold and often brilliant film-making: BRIAN VINER reviews Tom Cruise's latest film (pictured Ross Hatt and Tom Cruise)
Digger feels like a homage to Stanley Kubrick's 1964 masterpiece Dr Strangelove, with environmental disaster supplanting nuclear warfare as the principal threat to humanity (pictured John Goodman)
At the start, Digger has two pressing problems. His precious elderly cat, who shares his bed, has leukaemia. And his workforce, drilling in Greenland, are at mortal risk following a methane leak.
Characteristically, Digger is more concerned about his pet. His enormous baronial home might be festooned with the spoils of his hunting trips but his one true love is a dying cat.
Soon, though, the Greenland issue intensifies. Following a terrible explosion, a huge chunk of the polar ice shelf breaks off and appears to be heading for Europe at 'alarming velocity', with potentially cataclysmic consequences.
The autocratic US president (John Goodman) and his cabinet arrive at Digger's mansion to discuss the situation, explained to them by Digger's nervy head of environmental safety (Riz Ahmed).
All this is laceratingly satirical, with Goodman's President Compson whooping it up as a bad-tempered vulgarian, whose cabinet meetings resound with racism and sexism yet conclude with a clergyman leading prayers.
The not-unreasonable assumption that Compson might be modelled on an actual world leader, one eager to tap natural resources in Greenland and with 'drill, baby, drill' as his energy policy, encourages us to think we have the measure of the story.
Yet about half an hour in we are confounded by a major twist I will not divulge, not least because there are subsequent twists within the twist.
I should add that as an audaciously original story-teller, Inarritu has form, with credits including Birdman (2014) and The Revenant (2015), for which he won back-to-back Academy Awards for Best Director.
Yet with Digger he goes a step or two further. At the world premiere, Cruise described it as 'next-level filmmaking'. I can see what he means. Whether everyone will want to join him on the next level is another matter.
Digger feels like a homage to Stanley Kubrick's 1964 masterpiece Dr Strangelove, with environmental disaster supplanting nuclear warfare as the principal threat to humanity.
The film's main message, relayed via a bravura speech that Digger delivers to a grey assembly of European politicians, is that, as relentless consumers, we are all complicit in our own downfall.
I've already seen Digger twice, and enjoyed it much more the second time, knowing the twists from the start.
First time round, I felt it got tangled in its own conceit and artifice, becoming not just baffling but self-indulgent.
Nonetheless, this is bold and often brilliant film-making, with deserved whispers of Oscar nominations for Inarritu, Cruise and Goodman, and fabulous supporting performances from Ahmed, Sandra Huller and Jesse Plemons, not to mention an animatronic cat.
Digger is in cinemas from Friday

While congressional Republicans block efforts to ban Donald Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center, Department of Justice lawyers argue that the Trump-dominated institution is “already in a state of collapse both financially and physically” and nearly out of money to pay its bills.
On Monday night, Republican Sen. Mike Lee blocked bipartisan legislation to prevent the Trump administration from demolishing the venue after lawmakers drafted a bill in response to apparent threats that the building c ould be knocked down if the president isn’t allowed to add his name to it.
The Justice Department, meanwhile, told a federal appeals court that the beleaguered institution is “dangerously dilapidated, outdated and decrepit” while its finances are “equally in disrepair.”
On September 17 , a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to provide at least 30 days’ notice before making any physical changes to the Kennedy Center — including demolishing it — after the Trump-controlled board voted to shutter the venue for repairs.
The vote followed a judge’s ruling that blocked the Kennedy Center from adding the president’s name to the building after he repeatedly tried to rename the memorial after himself.
Kennedy Center officials insist that the venue is only “temporarily” closing to assess the “advanced deterioration,” fueling speculation that the president could try to tear it down altogether.
“Like many arts and entertainment facilities, the Center has been losing tens of millions of dollars each and every year for decades, and it is projected to lose around $100 million per year long into the future,” government lawyers wrote Tuesday .
“In short, both physically and financially, the Kennedy Center is in critical condition,” they added. “To bring this sick and poorly run facility back to health will require time, energy, talent, and large amounts of money.”
Congress appropriated roughly $258 million for capital restoration projects and renovations at the Kennedy Center last year. The Trump administration’s takeover, meanwhile, put the venue on track to a projected $23 million deficit, as ticket sales plunged and subscriptions fell under the leadership change.
Without “appropriate recognition” — such as putting Trump’s name on the building — the Kennedy Center will be “a financially insolvent facility and a decrepit, dilapidated, crumbling building, that is bleeding hundreds of millions of dollars in losses and that continues to race toward physical and financial ruin,” according to the government.
“The stakes are existential,” lawyers added. “Just this month, the Kennedy Center was only able to pay its bills thanks to [$17 million] raised by President Trump that were infused into the Kennedy Center account to keep it afloat.”
Those funds are “fast being expended” and will “dry up” without the president' s support, according to the filing.
Without Trump, the Kennedy Center will “continue its deterioration into an unsafe structure that will eventually collapse, with a determination to follow on how to proceed, and what to do with the site.”
Last month, after filing several court documents using increasingly hyperbolic and ominous language to keep Trump’s name on the building, the Justice Department floated the possibility that the building could be demolished altogether.
Bipartisan legislation spearheaded by Democratic Sen. Jeff Merkley and Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski sought to ban the demolition of presidential memorials. The senators lead the appropriations subcommittee that oversees funding for the center, the Interior Department and the National Park Service.
They sought to pass the bill by unanimous consent on Monday night, which would allow quick passage of a motion unless a single senator objects.
But Lee, a key Trump ally in the Senate, rejected the attempt.
“Trump’s threats to tear down the Kennedy Center — all because the law says he can’t put his name on the building — are straight out of the authoritarian playbook and should infuriate every American who values our history and the rule of law,” Merkley said in a statement.
Rep. Chellie Pingree, who is sponsoring a House version of the bill, said Trump’s threats are “beyond the pale.”
“This bill establishes a simple safeguard: if Congress created the designation, only an act of Congress can authorize its demolition,” she said.

The security alert issued by MI5 regarding a Chinese state-owned conglomerate accused of conducting espionage in the UK reveals the extent to which British intelligence remains concerned about Beijing’s influence, and risks casting a shadow over UK-China cooperation at a time when the bilateral relationship is enjoying a revival.
The UK’s domestic security service on Wednesday warned researchers and academics to cease work with the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), an organisation MI5 described as a “significant threat”.
The CAGT, which is also known as the China General Technology Research Institute, is accused of paying UK academics working in sensitive fields such as artificial intelligence and cybersecurity for “research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage”. The MSS is China’s Ministry of State Security, its intelligence agency.
China’s approach to intelligence gathering involves hoovering up vast amounts of data, often from unsuspecting individuals who believe they are participating in normal research or consultancy work.
This year the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warned businesses about Beijing-backed attempts to hack into everyday devices such as wifi routers.
Last year, MI5 issued another China-related security alert , warning parliamentarians about approaches from two LinkedIn profiles thought to be linked to Chinese intelligence.
Wednesday’s alert said academic institutions or researchers should be aware of the 2023 National Security Act , which makes it an offence to engage in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence agency. The warning is likely to send a chill through the UK’s cash-strapped higher education institutions, which have for years turned to China for funding and collaboration opportunities.
The UK is one of the leading countries to partner with China’s higher education sector. In May, China’s education ministry announced 219 new transnational education partnerships, with more than a fifth of the approvals being with British universities. That puts the UK at the top of the list of partner countries, ahead of Russia, France and Italy.
Chinese students are also the largest group of non-EU international students in the UK, generating about £600m a year for the higher education sector.
There has been growing concern in the UK that partnerships with China pose a risk to national security. The 2023 Intelligence and Security Committee report on China said UK academic institutions “provide a rich feeding ground for China to achieve both political influence and economic advantage” and flagged the risk of China “directing or stealing UK academic research”.
In this case, MI5 said that more than 100 academics linked to the UK had contributed to projects funded by the MSS via the front company. The areas of interest were AI, cybersecurity and steganography , the embedding of hidden data in pictures online.
Sam Goodman, the senior policy director at the China Strategic Risks Institute, said UK academics were “between a rock and a hard place” when trying to navigate areas of advanced interest that could be of interest to Chinese intelligence. “There is a lack of a coherent steer from government on something like AI. It isn’t particularly clear on AI at this juncture what levels of collaboration we can have with the Chinese,” Goodman said.
after newsletter promotion
Analysts say the UK should do more to highlight which areas are of potentially dual-use interest to Chinese intelligence and provide more guidance to universities and academics.
“It’s all very well issuing these warnings,” says Charles Parton, a senior fellow at the Royal United Services Institute. “Actually far more important, surely, is a consideration of which technologies can be cooperated with China, and which can’t.” He said naming specific Chinese companies as a risk would not help UK researchers to do due diligence on every potential partnership. “The Chinese are not stupid. If they want to hide the origin of someone, they’ll do it,” Parton said.
Meia Nouwens, a senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said more clarity was needed on the UK side to help guide researchers working in sensitive fields.
Nouwens said: “A problem has been that in the past there hasn’t been a great deal of discussion of what areas of research constitute a national security risk. Without understanding the limits are of what the UK seeks to protect, it is impossible to have a conversation about managing risk.”
The MI5 alert specifically accused the CAGT of being a front for China’s intelligence. But any research institution in China is ultimately controlled by the Chinese Communist party. “Research institutes that are conducting research on areas of strategic interest for China such as technology will have oversight from the party-state,” Nouwens notes.
That does not mean any collaboration with Chinese educational institutions is inherently dangerous, but it does mean UK academics working in sensitive fields will feel increasingly uneasy about working with a country that has financially underpinned the UK’s higher education sector for decades.

By MARK DUELL, DEPUTY CHIEF REPORTER (DIGITAL)
Published: 06:45 EDT, 30 September 2026 | Updated: 10:59 EDT, 30 September 2026
Prince Harry and Meghan today condemned 'extraordinarily reckless' international paparazzi who were seen looking into the grounds of their children's school.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex 's spokesman accused two photographers of an 'unacceptable intrusion into the privacy' of Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five.
The young men were wearing backpacks and using a white van when they were spotted circling the perimeter and monitoring children by private security and school staff.
In the wake of the suspected terror plot near RAF Fairford on Sunday, a representative for the couple said the photographers' actions displayed 'an extraordinary lack of judgment'.
A number of American children with families connected to the Gloucestershire airbase, which is also used by the US Air Force, are believed to attend the school.
The spokesman for the Sussexes said: 'The decision by photographers to conduct themselves in this way around a school is extraordinarily reckless.
'There is a world of difference between legitimate media activity and photographers walking the perimeter of a school, stopping to look into the grounds and monitoring children as they go about their day.
'It is concerning enough that certain European paparazzi appear unwilling to respect the privacy of children at school.
Harry and Meghan with their children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet in December 2025
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle at a David Foster Foundation event in Canada on August 7
'But to behave in this manner in these particular circumstances, and so soon after the incident at RAF Fairford, demonstrates an extraordinary lack of judgment.
'Whatever photographs they may have been seeking, this was not only an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children; it was an irresponsible and ill-considered way to conduct themselves in the vicinity of a school.'
The two men were initially seen separately and subsequently observed together before returning to a white van, which police later established was a rental vehicle.
Officers also then determined that they were international photographers working for a European press agency, which has not been named.
An insider told ITV News that the two men were seen 'scouting out' the children's school and 'doing reconnaissance' on it 'for a number of hours' before driving off.
The incident has been reported to the Executive Committee for the Protection of Royalty and Public Figures (Ravec), which is responsible for making decisions about royal security.
Harry and Meghan are waiting to hear the conclusion of Ravec's risk management board's threat assessment, which will determine whether the Sussex family should be entitled to taxpayer-funded security now they live in the UK.
The incident is understood to have taken place just 48 hours after five men were arrested near Fairford when a farmer discovered three vans blocking a road in the early hours of Sunday.
The base has been used in recent months by US bombers to launch air strikes against Iran.
Police officers guard an area near the RAF Fairford air base in Gloucestershire yesterday
Archie and Lilibet's education has already been an issue for the Sussexes, with the children moved to the new undisclosed school after just two days in class at a different institution.
The decision came after heavy traffic and the lengthy journey to the first school reportedly put their security team under strain.
The youngsters are believed to have been at their new school for around two weeks.
Harry said over the weekend that Archie and Lilibet are 'happy in school' and it is 'great' to be back in Britain – after returning a month ago following six years living in the US.
Of his return, the Prince added: 'It's been great. It's been great to be back on British soil.'
The Sussexes stepped down as working royals in 2020 for personal and financial reasons but rumours remain rife as to why they unexpectedly relocated to the UK from California.
Speculation ranges from the couple wanting their children to develop a closer relationship with their grandfather King Charles, Meghan seeking a return to acting and the Sussexes wanting to increase their profile.
In the run-up to their return, Charles was said to be glad to be able to spend more time with the family but remained adamant they would not be working royals, and there was no half-in, half-out option.
Within two weeks of arriving, there was reported pushback from Harry and Meghan after a letter, authorised by the King, was circulated by the Lord Chamberlain to senior stakeholders in the Government and military reiterating the couple were 'private citizens' and setting out guidance on how they should be treated.
The duke and duchess were said to be 'surprised' by the formal letter and the couple were reported to prefer the term 'public figures' instead.

Mattel on Wednesday named Roger Lynch as its new CEO and chairman, succeeding Ynon Kreiz.
Lynch, who has been a member of Mattel's board since 2018, will take the reins as chairman on Oct. 2 and CEO by Nov. 2, according to the press release .
Lynch is currently the CEO of Condé Nast, a position he has held since 2019. Mike Perlis will serve as Condé Nast's interim CEO while the board begins it search for Lynch's successor, according to a letter from Lynch.
"I am honored by the Board's confidence in me and couldn't be more excited to lead the incredible team at Mattel," Lynch said in the release. "Throughout my years on the Board, I have admired Mattel's brands, its talented people, and unique culture."
Kreiz will leave Mattel after more than eight years at the helm to take a senior leadership position at another public company.
He has led the toymaker and entertainment company through major transformations, including the release of "Barbie," which became the highest-grossing domestic film release of 2023 .
"It has been a privilege to lead Mattel, with a global team dedicated to its mission and purpose, and I am proud of all we have achieved together," Kreiz said in a statement. "Mattel is in a position of strength, with a world-class brand portfolio, product offering, and global capabilities."
Mattel has been working on bolstering its iconic brands, with Hot Wheels as a notable strength. The company is also attempting break into the digital games space in a bid to match rival Hasbro . It acquired full control of its Mattel163 Mobile Games Studio earlier this year.

articles.title_zh: Carnegie Mellon nets $3 billion gift, most ever given to a university
articles.content_orig:
Citadel CEO Ken Griffin announced Wednesday that he has committed $3 billion to Carnegie Mellon University, including $2 billion in funding to establish a new Miami campus.
The $3 billion pledge is the "largest individual gift in higher education history," according to a statement from the university, which called the gift "historic." The previous record was a $2 billion gift by Nike co-founder Phil Knight and his wife Penny to Oregon Health & Science University in August 2025.
Griffin, who is worth $57.5 billion by Bloomberg's estimate , will join Carnegie Mellon's board of trustees.
"The opportunity to bring Carnegie Mellon to Miami places our city at the heart of humanistic and scientific advancement and amplifies the University's international reach and impact," Griffin said in a release. "CMU Miami will cultivate the talent, knowledge, and expertise to launch new enterprises, contribute to Miami's economy and community, and advance the prosperity of our nation."
Previously, the hedge fund billionaire's largest donation was $300 million to Harvard University, his alma mater, in 2023. Griffin also contributed $125 million to the University of Chicago in 2017 when Citadel was still headquartered in the Windy City.
Since he moved Citadel's headquarters to Miami in 2022, citing concerns about crime in Chicago, he has become a vocal Miami booster, touting Florida's business-friendly policies, low taxes, and quality of life.
"It's a state that is prospering," he said at a CNBC conference in 2022 . "It's really fun to be in an environment where people are embracing the future. They're hopeful about the future."
In the past four years, Griffin has become a prolific philanthropist in South Florida. He's made gifts of $50 million apiece to the University of Miami's cancer center, the Baptist Health Foundation's neuroscience institute, and Success Academy, to fund the charter school network's expansion to Miami.
Carnegie Mellon's new Miami campus will span 35 acres in Wynwood, a neighborhood known for its art scene. Construction is slated to begin in 2027. The university expects to start enrolling students in 2028 and to support more than 3,500 students once the campus is complete.
The new campus's academic program will be organized around addressing societal challenges such as climate resilience and national security rather than academic majors, according to the release.
Griffin has been critical of leadership at elite universities, including his alma mater. In 2024, Griffin told CNBC's Leslie Picker that he had paused donations to Harvard over the university's response to antisemitism on campus and he also took verbal aim at top colleges.
"Are we going to educate the future members of the House and the Senate and the leaders of IBM? Or are we going to educate a group of young men and women who are just caught up in a rhetoric of oppressor and oppressee and this is not fair and frankly just like whiny snowflakes?" Griffin said.

China is not expected to materially boost its crude oil imports through the end of the year as oil prices surged above $100 per barrel again and independent refiners struggle to procure cheaper supply amid the near-disappearance of Iranian barrels.
China is on track to import roughly the same volumes of crude oil in September as it did in August, extending the trend of recovering shipments. However, the September-arriving cargoes were bought at oil prices in the $80s before the latest re-escalation in early September sent and kept Brent above $100 per barrel.
China’s crude oil imports rose for the second consecutive month in August as refiners turned to additional non-Middle Eastern supply and boosted overseas fuel shipments amid eased export restrictions.
The August import level was still 23.4% lower compared to the same month last year, but it’s a marked improvement from the June lows of just 7.1 million bpd.
China slashed its total crude oil imports to a decade low in June, culminating three months of very low import levels amid high prices and constrained supply from the Middle East.
September volumes are expected to be more or less around the August levels, but the outlook for the rest of the year has soured as oil is up above $100 per barrel again and the U.S. blockade is effectively eliminating the regular cheap supply on which China’s independent refiners relied for years to remain competitive.
The teapots now could start reducing refinery processing rates as oil prices rise and supply from major exporters such as Venezuela and Iran dries up as a result of U.S. foreign policy decisions.
Chinese state giants are not in a rush to buy much higher volumes of crude at above $100 a barrel with record-high freight costs, either, according to analysts.
“We don’t expect significant upside to China’s crude imports, partly as hefty premiums and expensive freight drive up the cost of feedstock, eroding margins,” Samuel Kong, senior oil analyst at FGE NexantECA, told Bloomberg .
Analysts at FGE NexantECA, as well as at Energy Aspects, have revised down their earlier projections of China’s crude oil imports in the fourth quarter, by about 400,000 barrels per day (bpd). Harry has continued pressing for protection, often drawing comparisons of what his wife has faced with that of his mother, Diana, who died in 1997 in a high-speed car crash while paparazzi were following her.
This latest incident comes as the couple are reportedly waiting on an official risk assessment now they have returned to the UK from Montecito, California.
The couple has been asked to provide authorities with as much detail as possible about their new daily routines, including trips such as the school run, addresses routinely visited, routes taken and more, according to The Telegraph newspaper earlier this month. By David Brunnstrom and Alexandra Alper
WASHINGTON, Sept 30 (Reuters) - The Republican chair of the congressional committee focused on China is calling on the Trump administration to scrutinize US ally South Korea's warming ties with China, which he said pose "significant risks" to the United States.
In a letter ‌to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Representative John Moolenaar urged "heightened vigilance" about the relationship, citing deepening leader-level ties, South Korean semiconductor investment in China, ‌and unfair treatment of American firms in South Korea compared with Chinese rivals.
Moolenaar described South Korea as "a major American ally," but warned of "the potential for frictions to develop into a structural shift in Seoul's ​alignment" requiring "close monitoring and, as necessary, concerted action."
South Korea's foreign ministry said it could not comment in detail on the contents of the letter, which was sent on Tuesday and has not been previously reported. It said that the US-South Korea alliance was the cornerstone of its foreign policy and that they were advancing the alliance across several areas.
The letter comes after a period of tensions in US-South Korea relations that has included some sharp criticism of Seoul by President Donald Trump.
The two countries have been allies ‌since the 1950-53 Korean War, in which China backed North ⁠Korea, but differences have surfaced over trade, China policy and security issues, even as Trump has worked to improve his own relations with Beijing.
It also comes as Seoul has pledged hundreds of billions of dollars in US-based investments.
On Tuesday, people familiar with the ⁠discussions told Reuters Trump could announce as soon as Wednesday that his administration intends to use South Korea's strategic investment fund for several major US projects including roughly $54 billion for a planned Alaska LNG facility.
Reuters has also reported that SK Hynix was considering leasing part of Intel's Ohio chip plant and even breaking ground on a new chipmaking facility for its ​subsidiary ​Solidigm.
Moolenaar called the pace of leader-level engagement between Seoul and Beijing unprecedented, citing Chinese President ​Xi Jinping's first visit to South Korea in 11 years in ‌2025 and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung's visit to China this year, the first by a South Korean president since 2019.
He said the "widening gulf" between South Korea and the US was especially troubling because Seoul had "effectively ruled out" supporting a regional response to any Chinese aggression against Taiwan, citing Lee's 2024 election campaign remark: "What does it matter to us what happens in the Taiwan Strait?"
In an interview with Japan's NHK broadcaster in January, Lee said that it would serve South Korea well to "avoid unnecessary involvement," saying it was in the national interest to respect others' positions.
This week, in a post on X mentioning South Korea's booming trade with China, Lee ‌said: "In diplomacy, South Korea-US alliance is most important, but it is also important to manage relations ​with China."
Lee met with Trump on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly last week, two ​days before the US president's meeting with Chinese leader Xi.
On technology, Moolenaar ​argued that South Korea's semiconductor investments in China could leave key US supply chains vulnerable to Chinese pressure. He pointed to Samsung's ‌chipmaking plant in Xi'an and SK Hynix's operations in Wuxi and ​Dalian, calling them potential points of leverage ​for Beijing over allied technology production.
Moolenaar also expressed concern over what he described as more lenient South Korean enforcement toward Chinese e-commerce platforms such as Alibaba's AliExpress and Temu when it came to alleged data privacy, consumer protection, cybersecurity and product safety violations compared with that faced by American firms ​such as Coupang.
The companies mentioned in the letter did not ‌immediately respond to requests for comment. Coupang declined to comment. South Korea's foreign ministry said its regulatory authorities treat all companies operating in ​Korea fairly.
Moolenaar called for a State Department briefing on developments in South Korea-China relations by October 31.
(Reporting by David Brunnstrom and Alexandra Alper; ​Additional reporting by Kyu-seok Shim in Seoul; Editing by Don Durfee and Michael Perry)

articles.title_zh: The US military says its withdrawal of troops from Iraq is complete
articles.content_orig:
BAGHDAD — The U.S. military announced Wednesday that it completed the withdrawal of all American troops from Iraq, ending a 12-year mission to fight the Islamic State group. The last U.S. troops left an air base in northern Iraq under a deal between Baghdad and Washington.
The withdrawal, agreed on two years ago, comes against the backdrop of the ongoing war between the United States and Iran that has also sometimes spilled over into Iraq, with Iran-backed militias firing on U.S. troops and the U.S. striking the groups’ strongholds.
In recent years, Washington has appeared to seek to shift its focus from the Middle East toward Asia, but that shift has been inconsistent, with the Pentagon alternating between reducing its Mideast presence and then finding itself engaging in new conflicts — including the ongoing war in Iran.
Baghdad touted the end of the U.S. mission as a sign of the country’s increasing strength and sovereignty.
The withdrawal was also celebrated by Iran-backed groups but raised concerns among some other Iraqis, particularly in the Kurdish region, where many fear a resurgence of the Islamic State group as well as more attacks by Iran-linked groups, possibly emboldened by the departure of U.S. forces.
Meanwhile, questions loom around the future of the Iraqi militias, which the Baghdad government has sought to disarm, with little success so far.
A new phase in Iraq after decades of U.S. involvement
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement that U.S. troops and equipment had completed an “orderly departure” from the air base in Irbil, in northern Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
“This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region,” he said. “It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship.”
He added that the U.S. military “will continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to our Iraqi partners.”
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over the handover ceremony and described the U.S. withdrawal as the beginning of a “new phase, one defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends.”
He said Iraqi security forces will continue the fight against IS and the government will ensure that non-state groups no longer hold weapons.
U.S. troops invaded Iraq in 2003 to topple Saddam Hussein. They departed in 2011, but three years later, Iraqi authorities invited a smaller U.S.-led mission to fight the Islamic State group, which had rampaged across Iraq, seizing large swaths of territory.
With the extremist group reduced to scattered sleeper cells, Washington and Baghdad agreed in 2024 to wind the mission down.
U.S. troops pulled out of bases in most areas of Iraq last year but maintained a small presence of hundreds of troops in the semiautonomous northern Kurdish region. Bases there have regularly come under attack since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran on Feb. 28. Iran-backed Iraqi militias also have coordinated with Yemen’s Houthi rebels to attack Saudi Arabia.
The future of militias remains unclear
The Iraqi government initially linked the Sept. 30 deadline for U.S. withdrawal to the disarmament of non-state armed groups by that date.
While a handful of less-influential militias have agreed to turn over their weapons, powerful groups close to Iran rejected the prospect or set conditions for disarming that the government would be unlikely to meet.
Al-Zaidi has since walked back the deadline. He told The New York Times earlier this month that the deadline for militia disarmament has been pushed to June 2027.
The effects of the U.S. withdrawal may not be immediately visible, particularly since the U.S. military presence had already been scaled down. But officials in Iraq’s Kurdish region have expressed anxiety about the departure and particularly about the removal of U.S. air defense systems.
The Kurdish regional government’s Peshmerga Ministry said the Kurdish region had faced more than 1,000 drone and ballistic-missile attacks during the recent U.S.-Iran conflict.
“The departure of the United States from the Kurdistan Region under these complex regional circumstances, without the provision of a defense system, is a matter of concern,” the statement said.
Iran-allied groups in Iraq, meanwhile, have celebrated the U.S. withdrawal.
“The expulsion of the occupation forces, defeated, from the land of Iraq is the beginning of full sovereignty,” Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, a security official with the powerful Kataib Hezbollah militia, said in a statement.
He added a warning to al-Zaidi and his government not to carry out American plans, threatening that “any government that does not work for the benefit of the people will be overthrown by all means.”
The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed militias, said in a statement that negotiations with the government over the regulation of weapons have not resulted in an agreement and that it was “not bound by any timeline or agreement” announced by the government or political entity. The group said it is open to “any dialogue that guarantees Iraq’s sovereignty and dignity.”

articles.title_zh: MLB Wild Card Series results: Scores, highlights and Game 1 playoff takeaways
articles.content_orig:
Whew! What a first day of playoff baseball that was on Tuesday. We had a clutch comeback in Georgia, a Pope-endorsed White Sox win in Houston, two Massachusetts natives dominating the Red Sox in the Bronx and a Michael King no-hit bid in San Diego.
Postseason Guide • Final bracket • Wild Card Series matchups • How to watch Wild Card Series on NBC, Peacock • Postseason schedule
Good news: We get to do it all again today.
We’ve got four more games, and each of them is an elimination game in this best-of-three format. Will we see four more games on Thursday? It depends how these four key questions are answered.
Phillies at Braves 2 p.m. ET, Peacock/NBC SP: Cristopher Sánchez (PHI) vs. Tyler Mahle (ATL)
Did the Braves just withstand the Phillies’ best shot?
The hope for the Phillies was that, with their whew! victory on the season’s final day, they’d be able to reset after a miserable week and essentially start over, fully focused on the only thing that matters to a veteran team like this: the postseason. And for 7 1/2 innings in Game 1, they pulled it off, getting timely hitting and some inventive (and slightly out-of-character) bullpen usage from interim manager Don Mattingly. The Truist Park crowd looked and sounded legitimately shook. Mattingly’s decision to call on star closer Jhoan Duran in the seventh inning against the Braves’ best hitters made sense, and you could even argue for the utility of keeping him out for the eighth -- this is a best-of-three series after all, every game is very important. But with one extremely misplaced fastball to Austin Riley in the bottom of the eighth, this whole series turned upside down.
White Sox at Astros 5 p.m. ET, Peacock/NBCSN SP: Sean Burke (CWS) vs. Hunter Brown (HOU)
Can Brown give the home fans something to cheer?
Here’s something that’s hard to believe but true: The Astros lost their eighth consecutive postseason home game on Tuesday, going back to Game 2 of the 2023 ALDS. Don’t forget: This is a team that won a World Series four years ago, their second in the past 10 years. But it’s also worth remembering that this Astros team isn’t the Astros teams we’ve grown used to seeing. They’re now four games under .500 at Daikin Park for the season. (And, ahem, one game under .500 anywhere for the season.) All the reasons the Astros have struggled this year were apparent in Game 1: They were short on pitching and they couldn’t put together much offense outside Yordan Alvarez.
There is some hope in Game 2, though. That starts with Brown. Last year’s third-place AL Cy Young Award finisher missed more than two months with a right shoulder strain early this season and was uneven after his return. But he had a 2.47 ERA over his final eight starts, three of which featured double-digit strikeouts. He also has been excellent against the White Sox this year, going 2-0 with a 1.38 ERA in two starts. Considering the Astros used eight pitchers Tuesday, including closer Josh Hader, they’re going to need Brown to carry them -- and he just might.
Red Sox at Yankees 8 p.m. ET, NBC/Peacock SP: Sonny Gray (BOS) vs. Max Fried (NYY)
Can the Sox end their month-long slump, against THIS pitching staff?
For all the talk of the Phillies’ September struggles offensively, the Red Sox were in even worse shape, scoring an MLB-low 71 runs for the month, or 18 fewer than the 29th-place Phils. Unfortunately for the Red Sox, it is still September. Cam Schlittler continued his dominance over them in Game 1 -- that ERA in six starts against Boston is now all the way down to 0.47 -- but the Red Sox weren’t any better against relievers Paul Blackburn and John Schreiber. The Yankees didn’t even have to deploy their highest-leverage bullpen arms, keeping them fresh for Game 2.
While Fried hasn’t been as great as Schlittler against them, he’s been pretty close, going 4-1 with a 1.93 ERA in seven career starts. Though you don’t have to be Schlittler or Fried to shut down the Red Sox right now. You know all that talk about the Yankees needing Aaron Judge? It turns out that they don’t need him that much if the opponent doesn’t score. The Red Sox are running out of time to get the bats going.
Cubs at Padres 10 p.m. ET, Peacock/NBCSN SP: Kevin Gausman (CHC) vs. Nick Pivetta (SD)
This isn’t going to be how PCA’s historic season ends … is it?
The last time someone not named Aaron Judge had a season with a FanGraphs WAR higher than Pete Crow-Armstrong’s 10.6 this year was 2004, when Barry Bonds put up an 11.5 (with a . 609 OBP. .609!). What PCA did in 2026 is going to go down as one of the best seasons this century, and one of the best seasons, if not the best season, in Cubs history. It was incredible.
It is also nine innings away from being over. And not just that: It’s nine innings away from another quiet playoff exit, something that may start to feel like part of PCA’s permanent record. After an 0-for-3 night (with a walk) in Game 1 -- including two strikeouts that had him growling at third-base umpire Bill Miller over check-swing calls -- he is 5-for-30 in his postseason career, including 0-for-his-last-11. Obviously, those numbers aren’t reflective of the year that PCA has had, or the player he is. But if he and the Cubs don’t turn it around on Wednesday, he’s going to have a long autumn and winter to try to remind himself of that.

articles.title_orig: Russia issues nuclear warning to NATO as tensions rise in the Baltic
articles.title_zh: Russia issues nuclear warning to NATO as tensions rise in the Baltic
articles.content_orig:
Russia has continued a bombardment on Ukraine's data centers and communications infrastructure as part of a fresh wave of attacks on the country's capital.
Ukraine's air force said Russian forces intensified strikes on Kyiv and other cities overnight by launching a mix of anti-ship and ballistic missiles, as well as dozens of jet-powered drones, which Ukrainian air defenses have struggled to intercept.
Russia's Defense Ministry said it struck several targets in Kyiv on Tuesday, including a locomotive depot housing a warehouse of FP-5 Flamingo ground-based missiles and their components.
The attacks also hit the Bi-mobile data center, which Russia's Defense Ministry said was one of Kyiv's main internet exchange points, and the Parkovy data center.
Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine's data centers and internet providers in recent days, seeking to disrupt the flow of information in the country. Ukrainian officials have expressed deep concern over the attacks, saying there is an urgent need for the country to be able to rapidly respond to missile and drone threats.
Ukraine, for its part, has sought to raise the cost of Russia's more than four-and-a-half-year war against it, targeting the country's oil refineries and logistics hubs .
Meanwhile, NATO on Tuesday denounced Russia's nuclear threats after publicly acknowledging a tense exchange with Moscow.
The military alliance said it made clear to Moscow that it is a "defensive alliance" and that none of its activities or exercises "pose a risk to any part of Russia."
NATO was responding to a warning issued by the Russian Embassy in Belgium on Monday that accused the alliance of escalating the situation around Kaliningrad, a small Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea.
The embassy said NATO's "reckless and irresponsible" approach regarding the strategic outpost, which is sandwiched between NATO member states Poland and Lithuania, heightens the risk of a direct military confrontation.
It added that Moscow was ready to use its entire military arsenal if NATO tried to block the region, according to Russian state news agency Tass.
"We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. We call on Russia to end its unprovoked war in Ukraine," a NATO spokesperson said in a statement shared with CNBC.
"Russia's use of hybrid tactics is a sign of desperation. But we will not be dissuaded from our support to Ukraine. We have what it takes to defend every inch of Allied territory and remain strong, ready, and able to counter any threat," they added.
The exchange reaffirmed the deep tensions in diplomatic relations since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
