articles.title_orig: iOS 26.7.1—Update Now Warning Issued To iPhone Users
articles.title_zh: iOS 26.7.1—Update Now Warning Issued To iPhone Users
articles.content_orig:
Attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-86950, an out-of-bounds write flaw, in an extremely sophisticated fashion, according to Apple.
Apple released new versions of iOS and macOS to address a zero-day vulnerability that a threat actor is actively exploiting in targeted attacks.
The out-of-bounds write vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-86950 , affects Apple's CoreGraphics framework, which macOS and iOS use to render and manipulate 2D graphics. The vulnerability affects a broad range of Apple devices, including iPhones dating back to the iPhone 11 and multiple generations of iPads.
The flaw has a CVSS score of 8.8 and can allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on an affected system. According to Apple's advisory , the vulnerability is being exploited "in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals" on versions of iOS before iOS 27. The technology giant said it has addressed the vulnerability by adding checks to ensure the software does not write data beyond the memory allocated for it.
Related: South Africa Seeks Help After Cyberattack Targets Air Traffic Control
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-86950 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog — a source that it wants organizations to use to prioritize patching efforts . In keeping with its binding operative directive (BOD 26-04) from earlier this year for high-priority vulnerabilities, CISA has given federal civilian executive branch agencies three days to apply Apple's recommended mitigation for the vulnerability. As per BOD 26-04, these agencies must also conduct a forensic triage by Oct. 2 to determine if they have already been compromised via CVE-2026-86950.
Apple credited Meta with disclosing the vulnerability to the company but has not released any information on the exploit activity or who it might be targeting.
Adam Bynton, enterprise security manager at Jamf, says CVE-2026-86950 is significant because it affects a component of the graphics stack used to process content across Apple's operating systems. Though Apple has only referenced the attacks as targeting iOS, the company has patched the same flaw in macOS Tahoe and Sequoia, Boynton points out.
“The broader pattern is worth watching," he says. "We continue to see highly sophisticated attacks look for routes through components that process untrusted content." As an example, he pointed to CVE-2025-55177 , a vulnerability in WhatsApp that attackers exploited in combination with CVE-2025-43300 , another out-of-bounds zero-day vulnerability, this time in Apple's ImageIQ technology.
"We have also seen Apple disclose targeted exploitation involving WebKit and other memory-safety vulnerabilities," Boynton says.
Related: AI Sandbox Escapes: Why Forensic Readiness Matters More Than Containment
That shouldn’t be interpreted as Apple devices being broadly insecure, he says. "Apple describes these attacks as highly sophisticated and targeted at a very small population, which is why separating targeted exploitation from everyday enterprise risk is important.”
It's unclear who is exploiting CVE-2026-86950 and if the attacks are ongoing. But Apple's description of the attacks as being extremely sophisticated hints that a nation-state actor or spyware firm might be involved. WhatsApp, for instance, has previously accused Israel's NSO Group of using its servers to distribute its Pegasus spyware on mobile devices belonging to targeted individuals.
Ensar Seker, chief information security officer at SOCRadar, says a memory-corruption vulnerability like CVE-2026-86950, which can lead to arbitrary code execution during file processing, creates the potential for a low-interaction or potentially zero-click attack chain when combined with an appropriate delivery mechanism.
The other important detail is Apple's description of the exploitation as an "extremely sophisticated attack" against specific individuals, he says. "That language generally points toward highly targeted operations rather than broad cybercrime," he adds. "Organizations should therefore treat this less like a theoretical vulnerability and more like an indication that advanced threat actors continue to invest heavily in finding ways around Apple's security architecture."
Related: SectopRAT Returns, Hiding Inside a Legitimate Application
The trend is not simply that Apple has more vulnerabilities, Seker continues. What stands out is the continued discovery of flaws being used in sophisticated exploit chains targeting devices that many organizations have traditionally viewed as lower-risk endpoints.
"Over the past year, we have seen exploited vulnerabilities involving WebKit, media and image processing, privilege escalation, authorization controls, and memory corruption," Seker says. "Attackers are increasingly looking for chains rather than a single vulnerability: One flaw provides initial code execution, another escapes a sandbox or increases privileges, and additional components establish access to sensitive information."
The fact that Apple devices are strategically important endpoints at many enterprises, and many high-value targets frequently use iPhones and Macs, also makes the economics of developing exploits targeting Apple vulnerabilities more attractive. The first priority for organizations therefore is to reduce patch latency for Apple products. "When Apple identifies active exploitation, security teams should treat the update as an emergency security patch rather than waiting for the normal monthly patching cycle," Seker says.Organizations should also bring Apple devices fully into their enterprise security program and stop treating them as inherently secure endpoints simply because of Apple's security architecture. "Enterprises need centralized device management, enforced OS minimum versions, rapid update policies, visibility into device compliance, and controls that prevent outdated devices from accessing sensitive corporate resources," he says.

articles.title_orig: Ted Lasso's Annette Badland Reflects On Mae's Journey With The Lady Greyhounds In Bittersweet Episode 9
articles.title_zh: Ted Lasso's Annette Badland Reflects On Mae's Journey With The Lady Greyhounds In Bittersweet Episode 9
articles.content_orig:
"Ted Lasso" packed plenty into its penultimate Season 4 episode: Keeley learned that she's pregnant and expecting her first child with Roy, while viewers learned that Zelda, not Rebecca's ex-husband Rupert , is trying to steal Richmond out from under her. (The episode concluded with a tribute card honoring the late Anthony Head , who played Rupert in Seasons 1-3 but did not appear in Season 4.)
But the hour's most bittersweet story belonged to Mae, who spent what would turn out to be her final day alongside the Lady Greyhounds. The Crown & Anchor proprietor rode the bus with the team, joined them in the locker room, and revealed that she'd once dreamed of becoming a professional footballer herself — an opportunity that simply didn't exist for women in her day. "You're talented. You belong on that pitch," she told the players before watching them overcome a 2-0 deficit to win 4-2. Later, Rebecca received word that Mae had passed away and broke the news to Ted.
In the Q&A below, Annette Badland — who has recurred since Season 1 — reveals when she learned of Mae's fate, reflects on what the women's team meant to her character, and discusses Mae's poignant final day.
TVLINE | Did you know heading into Season 4 that Mae was going to pass away, or was that something you were told or discovered close to when you received the script for Episode 9? Closer to when I received the script. Quite a shock. But what a privilege to have been in it at all. And she got to fulfill things she hadn't done — being with the team and being on the bus and being part of things, because she cares so much about it. I thought that was a terrific way [to conclude her storyline].
And Jason told me himself. He was very honorable and came to my room and talked to me about it. And then, from the conversation we had after that, he adapted his storyline in [Episode] 10, but I can't really tell you about that.
TVLINE | Mae had so many wonderful moments over these four seasons. Obviously, she was especially joyful this year with the creation of the women's team, and there was one specific shot in Episode 3, when we first see the Lady Greyhounds play, of Mae in the stands, and you can just feel how elated she was to be there for that first game. What did it mean to you to see this new team give Mae such a renewed sense of excitement and purpose this year? Absolutely tremendous. I mean, the girls are wonderful — the actresses — and certainly when we did the pub quiz scene, it was like a tidal wave coming into the pub. It took two days to shoot, and they just were so effervescent and filled the building.
I, Annette, support the lionesses. I think it's tremendous what's happening with women's football. Mae grew up at a time, as did I, when women couldn't play football. I'm sure you know all of this — they were banned. And she would have liked to have played herself, but never could or did. And so, this is enormous for her. Huge. As a woman, that that's attainable now is tremendous.
TVLINE | I was going to ask about that pep talk Mae gives the team. Because it's such a wonderful coda on Mae's arc. Not only does she get to share her history and her love of the game, and what she couldn't do that these women can do now, but she gets to tell them, "You're talented. You belong on that pitch." What did it mean to you to get to punctuate Mae's arc that way? I think it's tremendous that Jason allowed that. He cares about the women's game, and he cares about his characters. So to develop that — to not just put her on the bus, which is very jolly and wonderful, but to have that moment — is really significant. She's not just a bystander. She actually gets involved.
TVLINE | As you said, Mae spent her final day riding the bus with the Lady Greyhounds. She joins them in the locker room. She watches them pull off this incredible comeback. Do you think Mae died happy — and that, in some ways, this was exactly how she would have wanted to spend her last day? Yeah, I think this is the best passing she could possibly have. Really, it's tremendous. Not that she would want to go, but to see them develop.... Yes, it would be terrific.
TVLINE | We see some of the immediate fallout: Rebecca learning that Mae passed, Rebecca telling Ted... and even though we don't hear Rebecca, we immediately see this grief wash over Ted. What does it mean to you to see how much this woman, this character, had come to mean to both of them — and, by extension, to Richmond? I was very moved by it because I didn't anticipate it, I suppose. But Mae and Ted have been more involved this season, and she's made a connection with his son. So, it's important to me as an actor that that was there for her.
Jason often talked about her being the matriarch. And although she was effervescent and loudmouthed, she was also a lioness. It took a lot to win her trust and affection, but once you did, she would protect you. So that that was noticed and appreciated. There was a connection. She wasn't simply another person on the journey. It was very specific. So Annette is very pleased that he felt that was correct.
TVLINE | What will you miss most about being part of "Ted Lasso" and the experience you've had making this show? I'm very proud to be part of it because of the public response. I'll miss the laughter and the camaraderie. But I get messages from people who say, "My mother has cancer. She goes for her treatment, she comes home, she's in a terrible state. We all pile on the bed and we watch 'Ted Lasso,' and we laugh and we believe." So to be involved with something that can do that is a huge gift, and I will miss it desperately. But I know that's in the world, so it's terrific.
TVLINE | The Crown & Anchor, aside from Nelson Road, is perhaps the most iconic set of "Ted Lasso." A lot of your scenes were obviously spent there. I know that when a series wraps, one of the common questions cast members get asked is, "Did you take anything from set?" Obviously, this show isn't over, but do you have any sort of souvenir — something that you took from that set that you'll have with you to cherish after this experience? I still have my "w–ker" badge, but I've had that a while. I was given something that was on the set. I didn't steal it. I can't really tell you, but it's one of the reasons Ted thought about coming back [to coach the women's team]. It's at the beginning of this [season], and it figures in [Episode] 10, and it was given to me. But I'm not going to spoil it for you.
TVLINE | Mae was featured so prominently this season. You had such a lovely scene with Jeremy Swift in Episode 8, echoing "All the President's Men." Do you have a favorite scene from this four-season run? No, but I liked the development [this season]. There was more development in it, so I was relishing each of the scenes as they came along, and different stories were being told. There wasn't really a specific scene. The locker room is important, but I enjoyed the women, the bus — just for her, that freedom, that sharing. Yeah, those scenes, I suppose. Don't tell the lads in the pub, though!
TVLINE | You have my word. [ Laughs ]

articles.title_zh: Trump says top tech firms have signed accord to 'self-police' AI development
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump speaks to reporters at the White House in Washington, Tuesday Sept. 29, 2026, after meeting with top executives of AI firms, as House Speaker Mike Johnson of La., and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang listen. Jacquelyn Martin/AP hide caption
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Tuesday said that he and a large group of leaders of artificial intelligence companies had signed a voluntary accord that will include internal and external reviews during a meeting at the White House aimed at addressing Americans' fears about the technology.
"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference outside the West Wing.
Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson met with leading executives from top tech firms that are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI infrastructure, including data centers in communities across the country, which have sparked grassroots, bipartisan opposition.
The accord was signed by Trump, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Elon Musk, founder of xAI, which is now part of SpaceX.
The accord, which Trump posted on his social media site, Truth Social, late Tuesday, opened the door to future regulation but focused on four voluntary steps for the companies to take.
The accord said the companies would implement "robust internal controls," partner with an "independent external auditor" to assess whether the controls were working, and establish a committee within each company's board of directors to evaluate reports from internal and external auditors.
"Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws and regulations," the accord said.
Trump repeatedly praised the business executives for developing a technology that he said would produce "unbelievable growth." Investment in data centers and the accompanying computer equipment has accelerated the economy and boosted the stock market, which has swelled investment accounts for higher-income Americans and lifted their spending.
Yet there were some notes of caution Tuesday. Amodei, who has been one of the most outspoken voicescalling for a slowdown in AI development, said, "The technology has very real risks."
"And, you know, the mechanism, how we address those risks is still under discussion," Amodei said.
Trump suggested that about 10 people would be named to a committee to "watch over the whole enterprise" and said the accord would be "morally binding." He also said he would name someone to oversee the agreement in coming days after consulting with industry.
Some of the actions outlined in the accord are measures these companies are already taking in some form or have previously committed to doing.
The intention of the accord balances the latitude needed for innovation with regulation, said Shri Narayanan, a university professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Southern California. That innovation is not just limited to improving the capabilities of these AI models, Narayanan said, but also to efforts to improve model safety and security.
Other experts are skeptical of putting "so much faith in self-policing," like Robin Jia, an assistant professor of computer science at the University of Southern California. Jia said it's crucial to ensure the leading labs' intentions are "well-aligned with the broader interest of the American public." He pointed to the recent disclosures of hacking incidents and said: "As the models get better, the consequences of such things are only going to get greater."
Some also took issue with the accord's vague, broad language. Alex Pascal, executive director of the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society, said: "The only way to reduce the risks and harms of AI to Americans is through robust legal liability, regulation and fundamentally changing the race dynamics that are driving unsafe decision-making by frontier AI developers whose costs are borne by the American people."
Huang sat to Trump's right during a White House luncheon meeting, according to a seating chart the president posted on Truth Social. Musk sat to Trump's left.
Earlier Tuesday, Trump promised that the U.S. government wouldn't limit the development of artificial intelligence or support calls for "guardrails" or other restrictions.
"I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," Trump said at the unveiling of an AI chatbot, America.gov, intended to help Americans navigate government services. "We can't stifle it, and we're leading by a lot."
The unveiling of the AI government chatbot occurred at a daylong event in Washington during which multiple Trump administration officials celebrated a "Golden Age" fueled by what Trump insists on calling "super intelligence," rather than artificial intelligence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio highlighted that the chatbot at America.gov could soon be used to apply for a first-time passport fully online, without the in-person visit to a processing center currently required.
Trump also said the executives had agreed to assuage the bipartisan opposition to data centers cropping up in local communities across the country by providing more financial support to local schools or taking steps to reduce energy costs.
"You're going to see, data centers are going to be very popular," Trump said. If the opposition continued, Trump suggested, "they'll be forced to go overseas or other locations."
Also Tuesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in a television interview that the company is increasingly focused on safety. The day before, his company halted the rollout of a new model over safety concerns.
"We are pacing our progress, which includes sometimes not training a model," he said on CNBC. "We have to do these in a way where we can make very confident safety cases and claims, so that people don't have a bunch of anxiety."
For his part, Trump on Tuesday portrayed the race to develop AI as largely a global competition between the United States and China. He said there would be a winner and a loser, with no "second place."
The two countries agreed last week to establish a channel for handling AI-related incidents during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington. But Trump underscored Tuesday that he didn't want to cooperate too much with China: "I didn't want to do anything, because we're leading. Why would I want to do anything?"

By JAMES TAPSFIELD, UK POLITICAL EDITOR
Published: 02:38 EDT, 30 September 2026 | Updated: 05:40 EDT, 30 September 2026
Andy Burnham is facing a Labour backlash as he hints at going 'all the way' and pledging to rejoin the EU.
The PM used his big conference speech yesterday to blame Brexit for many of the country's problems, saying he will spell out options for the future at a summit with Brussels later this year.
But the move has sparked concerns among his own troops, with Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra warning returning to the bloc is 'unrealistic'.
The stance also represents a dramatic U-turn from May, when Mr Burnham told a conference in Leeds: 'I am not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU.
'I respect the decision that was made at the referendum and it is going to undermine everything I have said about strengthening democracy if we don't respect that vote.'
In interviews after his speech yesterday, Mr Burnham told the BBC he did not want to leave the issue 'hanging' and he wanted to be clear on 'where we want Britain to go in the next decade'.
Asked whether he wanted the UK to rejoin the bloc, he told Radio 4's Today programme he wanted to 'look at the options'.
Andy Burnham is facing a Labour backlash as he hints at going 'all the way' and pledging to rejoin the EU
'We could stay as we are. That's definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay,' he told the programme.
'We could look at what (former Conservative chancellor) George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market or we could go all the way.'
Labour's election manifesto in 2024 ruled out joining a customs union, going back into the single market or allowing the return of freedom of movement with the EU.
But Mr Burnham has indicated he is prepared to recommend going beyond those red lines in future.
'There are clearly options that need to be considered, and we have to look at what is doable and what would be the pros and cons of each,' he told the BBC.
He said the need for a debate about the UK's future relationship with Europe was part of his plan to shift the country in a new direction.
'We've been in a rut. The country hasn't been working for people as it should,' he told BBC Breakfast.
Tory Deputy Leader Alex Burghart said: 'You cannot trust a word Andy Burnham says.
'Just a few weeks ago he said he wanted to move on from the Brexit arguments and now he is dragging Britain back into them by floating the prospect of rejoining the EU.
'Labour cannot blame a democratic vote from over a decade ago for the consequences of their own economic decisions. While they look backwards, the Conservatives will look forwards.'

articles.content_orig:
PM says he is looking at all options and ministers will examine ‘what is doable’ and the ‘pros and cons’
UK politics live – latest updates
Andy Burnham has opened the door to the UK rejoining the EU, saying Britain could “go all the way”, as he prepares to reconsider Labour’s post-Brexit red lines.
The prime minister used a series of interviews after his emotional Labour conference speech to spell out how wide-ranging his consideration of Britain’s future with Brussels could be because Brexit had caused “more harm than good”.
Burnham said the government could keep the current arrangements, seek a customs union, return to the single market or “go all the way” in what would be full EU membership. Speaking to the BBC, he said ministers would examine “what is doable” and the “pros and cons” of each option.
Asked whether he wanted the UK to rejoin the bloc, the prime minister told Radio 4’s Today programme he wanted to “look at the options”. He added: “We could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay. We could look at what George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market or we could go all the way.”
It is a significant shift from the position Labour fought the 2024 election on. Its manifesto explicitly ruled out returning to the EU single market or customs union, as well as restoring freedom of movement.
A customs union would bring Britain much closer to the EU on trade in goods. The UK and EU would apply the same tariffs to imports from elsewhere, removing trade barriers businesses have faced after Brexit . But it would not on its own put Britain back inside the wider single market or remove every border check.
If Britain were to rejoin the single market, it would be a significant step with the country having to accept closer alignment with EU rules.
“There are clearly options that need to be considered, and we have to look at what is doable and what would be the pros and cons of each,” Burnham told the BBC.
Although Burnham has not set out any timetables or specifics, to “go all the way” would mean considering EU membership. He went further in his interviews on Wednesday than his conference speech in which he told delegates Britain could not keep avoiding a decision about its long-term relationship with its largest trading partner.
The prime minister has vowed to set out different choices facing the country around the time of the UK-EU summit in November. “We’ve been in a rut. The country hasn’t been working for people as it should,” he told BBC Breakfast. The summit was originally supposed to take place in July under Keir Starmer but was postponed after his resignation.

While Britain will take part in the Erasmus + scheme again in 2027, the EU has authorised talks at the summit on closer electricity-market links, with negotiations on food trade and youth mobility still under way.
Burnham argued in his conference speech that leaving the EU had weakened Britain’s cooperation with EU countries on migration and said the summit would assess how the two parties could work more closely. “We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of the century until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market,” Burnham said in his speech on Tuesday in Liverpool.
“I cannot say to you that where we are is good enough. Brexit has done more harm than good. So I will take the opportunity around the [UK-EU] summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners. And there are different options.”
The prime minister was more cautious when pressed on help households could receive in the budget given the looming winter and rising energy and fuel costs. Burnham said he was considering “everything that might help people” including whether to scrap panned fuel duty increases.
“The question I’ve got is: ‘How many can I afford?’” he told BBC Breakfast. The chancellor, John Healey, has said “fiscal discipline” will be at the heart of his budget despite facing calls to offer people more help with the cost of living.

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., discusses President Donald Trump’s meeting with artificial intelligence leaders at the White House and the signing of the White House Accord on SI on ‘The Bottom Line.’
President Donald Trump on Tuesday signed an executive order directing the federal government to replace the term "artificial intelligence" with "Super Intelligence" across the executive branch, cementing a rebranding effort he has championed in recent weeks.
Signed after a White House summit with leading technology executives, the order directs federal agencies to use the terms "Super Intelligence" and "SI" in official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents and other non-statutory materials.
The order also directs agencies to "no longer acknowledge" the terms " artificial intelligence " and "AI," according to the White House.
The order further instructs the assistant to the president for science and technology to develop a federal definition of SI and recommend any additional executive actions needed to implement the new terminology.
TRUMP TO MAKE SURPRISE STOP AT TEXAS TRUCK FACTORY TO TOUT MANUFACTURING
President Donald Trump on Tuesday signed an executive order directing the federal government to replace the term "artificial intelligence" with "Super Intelligence" across the executive branch. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
Trump argued in the order that AI no longer reflects the technology's rapidly advancing capabilities, saying SI better captures its promise and potential.
"The term 'Super Intelligence' more appropriately captures the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies," Trump wrote.
He also wrote that modern AI systems are increasingly amplifying human ingenuity and unlocking new forms of creativity, arguing they represent the beginning of a new era of SI.
The order follows remarks Trump made at last week's United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), where he publicly called for replacing the term "artificial intelligence" with SI.
TRUMP SAYS HE APPROVED NEW FUEL ECONOMY STANDARDS ENDING BIDEN-ERA ELECTRIC VEHICLE MANDATE
Trump signed the executive order after a White House summit with leading technology executives. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
"Whoever wins AI, you have to remember this, and now I say whoever wins SI, whoever wins superintelligence, wins. That's the group that wins," Trump said at the time.
The executive order also comes as governments and technology companies continue debating how rapidly advancing AI systems should be governed.
During a White House roundtable with tech executives, Trump, who has opposed imposing formal guardrails on SI, said participants signed a document at the conclusion of the gathering.
Trump added that the document, dubbed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, is "morally binding" for the executives who signed it.
"They almost viewed it as a separate kind of constitution," Trump said of the tech leaders. "When they signed that, it meant a lot."
TRUMP REBRANDS AI, REJECTS 'GLOBALIST SCHEME' TO CONTROL TECH
After the summit, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X Tuesday that he viewed the summit as a "positive step." (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
After Tuesday's White House summit, House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said participants focused on striking "the right balance" between "the interests of the American people," advancing technology and maintaining the United States' competitive edge over China .
"This is a statement of principles that you'll see, a statement of standards, commitments that are voluntary on behalf of the industry. It sets forth expectations," Johnson said. "It's, in short, summary, robust internal controls and layers of internal and external review."
Tuesday evening, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X that he viewed the summit as a "positive step."
"I think it's a significant positive step that the leaders of every major American lab have committed to implementing robust internal controls and multiple layers of audits and reviews," Zuckerberg wrote.

articles.content_orig:
Beijing plans to double down on basic research, cutting-edge technologies and scientific talent as it strives to achieve tech self-sufficiency
For the first time, China’s spending on research and development as a share of gross domestic product has surpassed the average for Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) members – a trend one analyst expects to continue as Beijing seeks to strengthen technological self-reliance amid intensifying global competition.
R&D expenditure exceeded 3.92 trillion yuan (US$584.8 billion) in 2025, accounting for 2.8 per cent of GDP, Science and Technology Minister Yin Hejun said at a press conference on Tuesday. The OECD average stood at 2.7 per cent for the year, the National Bureau of Statistics reported.
Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, said the achievement showed how China’s investment in innovation had reached a level comparable to that of developed economies. He expected the share of GDP devoted to R&D to keep rising, with a greater focus on optimising funding allocation and improving research efficiency.
“We must continuously increase the proportion of investment in basic research to build a solid foundation for ‘zero-to-one’ original breakthroughs,” Wang said, while ensuring that “large-scale R&D investments translate more efficiently into industrial competitiveness”.

articles.title_orig: Man City’s ‘sham contracts’, spending breaches and ‘disguised funding’: Breaking down the findings
articles.title_zh: Man City’s ‘sham contracts’, spending breaches and ‘disguised funding’: Breaking down the findings
articles.content_orig:
Published: 14:33 EDT, 29 September 2026 | Updated: 15:47 EDT, 29 September 2026
It is an episode which illustrates the struggle there has been in extracting transparency and truth about Manchester City , whose relentless, bullying corporate machine has looked to shut down investigation and inquiry through years of deceit.
Eight years ago, I wrote a story, published by The Independent, whom I worked for at the time, about an obscure and puzzling company called Fordham Sports Image Rights, to which City had supposedly sold the club’s future image rights for £24.5million – a sum they needed to avoid breaching financial sustainability rules in the 2012-13 season.
City had made no secret of earning this figure. They stated it in their annual accounts. Yet Fordham’s directors, detailed in their Companies House listing, were City’s very own legal officer Simon Cliff and non-executive director John MacBeath – a qualified chartered accountant.
Fordham clearly had a very distinct link to the club. And when I made more inquiries about City selling off those image rights to such a firm, there were blank looks. Several sources confirmed to me that, contrary to this notion, City were still raking in millions from those deals.
The sources were significant people. A Spanish financier Esteve Calzada, chief executive of Saudi club Al Hilal these days, who as an adviser to City at that time had negotiated image rights deals for Kevin De Bruyne and others, said he was working for the club itself.
Calzada, a good friend of City chief executive Ferran Soriano, told me: ‘I’ve always been working on a commercial arrangement with the club. We help the club bring in deals.’
My sources on the Fordham story included an adviser to City chief executive Ferran Soriano (right, pictured with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak)
Those controlling City’s information are not the only ones you go up against when challenging the notion of Sheikh Mansour (centre) as a beneficent altruist
The detail might seem arcane and dry. The small financial details get crushed these days in the stampede for the next soundbite or headline. But it was fundamental to City's attempts to comply with the rules set out for any teams wishing to compete in the Champions League, at a time when UEFA were investigating the club.
We published the article. ‘Manchester City earning millions from image rights after telling UEFA investigators they had sold them,’ our headline stated.
The full force of Manchester City’s lawyers came down on us in a way which I have not experienced in more than 30 years in this business. There was an immediate threat to sue. A demand from the specialist internet law firm City employed that the digital piece be removed. That an apology for it be published. And that I personally tweet out that apology. It would have been an unprecedented level of 'contrition'.
Ours was not a big operation. As I recall, the managing editor who fielded this, Will Gore, was juggling 1001 tasks and did not have a sea of lawyers in the next office. But we were not cowed. A detailed, 1,500-word defence of the story was sent in return. We waited. And we waited. And we heard no more from Manchester City or their specialist internet lawyers.
In November 2018, a cache of documents extracted by hacker Rui Pinto, and subsequently published, suggested that we actually only had half of the story.
City's owners, Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) were in fact financing Fordham, according to the leaks – effectively paying part of the players' wages through the shell company which had paid City the £24.5m for the ‘image rights’. Not only were City boosting their income against the rules but reducing their headline wage bill as they did so.
Of course, those controlling City’s information are not the only ones you go up against when challenging the fluffy PR notion of Sheikh Mansour as a beneficent altruist. Many's the time that their weaponised supporters have dispensed filth on social media. They still will.
Last Friday’s revelation that City had been found guilty on all but one relatively inconsequential charge was justification for all who have seen through City’s deceit and questioned the absurd notion that they are the victims of some Manchester United and Liverpool led ‘red cartel’.
And, let it be said, justification for the staff of the Premier League, for whom this experience has not been easy. The Premier League, more than any, have refused to be intimidated.
Staff at the Premier League, including CEO Richard Masters, have remained steadfast in their pursuing of the City case despite outside pressure
But when the League’s explosive and utterly damning statement was published late on Tuesday afternoon, there, in the relatively brief summary of how the club had artificially reduced its costs by £900million over nine seasons, was the name: ‘Fordham.’
It was detailed as one of the ‘sham arrangements’, entered into to enable City to ‘record lower operating expenses than it actually incurred.’ Yes, the statement related, there had been ‘a “sham” circular arrangement with Fordham.'
This was a rather more succinct and emphatic way of putting it than we accomplished in November 2018 for an article that was never removed and is still very much there . We were right all along and despite the mess, waste and ugliness of this interminable case, there is a sweet kind of vindication about that.

articles.title_orig: Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice, 2 stars with Boston roots, lead Yankees to statement win over the rival Red Sox
articles.title_zh: Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice, 2 stars with Boston roots, lead Yankees to statement win over the rival Red Sox
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK — Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice are from Massachusetts. More importantly for the New York Yankees , they're damn good baseball players.
Both Massholes delivered massive performances on Tuesday in Game 1 of the 2026 wild-card series against the Boston Red Sox . Schlittler tossed 6 1/3 scoreless and punched out 10. Rice went 4-for-5 with 2 homers and 6 RBI. The Yankees clobbered their forever rivals 9-0 in a laugher to put themselves one win from advancing to an ALDS date with the Tampa Bay Rays .
For most of this picturesque autumn night in the Bronx, Schlittler was the main character. It was the second consecutive postseason in which New York's flame-throwing string-bean right-hander gave his boyhood team a baseball swirly. The presumptive AL Cy Young surrendered just two hits — one to the second batter he faced and one to the last. Otherwise, Schlittler was nearly flawless, with a fifth-inning free pass to Jarren Duran the only blemish.
He did so with a barrage of curveballs, 32 to be exact, 12 more than he'd thrown in any other MLB start. That pitch-mix pivot kept Sox hitters guessing and led to a whopping 24 whiffs against Schlittler. The dominance was so striking that New York's outfielders — Cody Bellinger , Spencer Jones and Heliot Ramos — each handled the baseball just once while Schlittler was on the mound.
"It's insane, bro," Jones told Yahoo Sports postgame. "Obviously I'm locked in, ready to make plays and whatever, but six or seven pitches will happen with Cam, and I won't even think about it. I got one fly ball. Didn't touch another one."
"It's kinda boring sometimes," Ramos joked. "Like, is it time to go home yet?"
Nobody in attendance, Red Sox hitters included, was shocked to see the Yankees ace toss a gem. All season, Schlittler has bullied opponents with triple-digit heat, three unique fastballs, a dastardly curveball and the spiteful aggression of a more aggrieved man. Few batted an eye when the third pitch out of his hand clocked in at 101 mph. But when the 2022 seventh-round draft pick reemerged from the Yankees' dugout for the seventh inning, with 107 pitches already on his ledger, a gleeful, unexpected roar reverberated around the ballpark.
A few batters later, Schlittler was done, but the night was his nonetheless. He finished with 117 pitches, the most by a Yankee in a postseason start since CC Sabathia way back in the 2012 ALDS. Simply put: Pitchers don't really do that anymore. In the era of big velocity and deep bullpens, teams rarely let starters wander far past the 100-pitch mark. In fact, the only other 117-pitch playoff start since 2019 was Garrett Crochet 's wild-card Game 1 performance against the Yankees last year in this very ballyard.
That one was a crowd-silencer. This one was a lot more thunderous.
"Any time he's going out there, he's got the most confidence," catcher Austin Wells said of Schlittler. "Now, back to back years, great outings against them in the playoffs. That's just what he's going to do."
It was clear leading into Tuesday's showdown that Boston's offensive approach against Schlittler would revolve around working deep counts and grinding out at-bats. Red Sox skipper Chad Tracy said as much during his Monday media conference. Maybe they wouldn't rain runs on Schlittler's head, but they could certainly attempt to outlast him in a war of attrition. After all, only one qualified MLB starter allowed foul balls at a higher rate this year. Drag Schlittler into the mud, force him to the showers after five, and Boston could take its best shot against the underbelly of New York's bullpen.
The second Boston hitter of the night, catcher Adley Rutschman , used that strategy to perfection. He worked a 10-pitch plate appearance against Schlittler before dunking a single into left. It was the type of battle that threatened to shorten the hurler's evening. Yet Schlittler kept on pitching, kept on blowing gas by a carousel of overmatched Red Sox. By the time Boston got a clean frame against a more mortal arm, they faced too steep a climb — a four-run deficit with just six outs to go.
That strong Yankees advantage was mostly Rice's doing. He smoked a solo shot to dead center in the fifth, doubling New York's lead to two. A few innings later, Rice laced a single into right and plated the third Yankees run. Then, in the eighth, Rice delivered the final blow: a no-doubt grand slam into the home bullpen that sent Yankee Stadium into full, ear-splitting revelry.
Much has been made about Schlittler's and Rice's Massachusetts origins, how Rice grew up a Yankees fan in Sox country, how Schlittler pours fuel on his competitive fire by sparring with Sox fans online. But the real story is how two overlooked, late-drafted, small-school college players developed into franchise-altering monsters. Schlittler was a seventh-rounder out of Northeastern; Rice went in the 12th from Dartmouth. Besides, none of the players in Boston's clubhouse care that the two dudes who kicked their butts on Tuesday happen to be from Massachusetts.
It's no surprise, then, that when asked about Schlittler's and Rice's New England connection after the game, Boone directed his answer toward otherwise forgotten chunks of the 2021 and 2022 MLB drafts.
"Pretty remarkable. I mean, not two top-draft-pick guys. Obviously with strong Massachusetts ties. Obviously, that's been a storyline for a couple of years now," he said. "For them to go out and have that kind of night together to start this postseason, pretty amazing."
Schlittler conveyed a similar sentiment. "Mid-round guys ..." he said. "Just to have the confidence of being mid-round guys, having to work a little bit harder to get up here and embrace that together, it's special."
It's also a testament to the Yankees' scouting and development operation. Every single MLB organization had access to Schlittler and Rice. For all of New York's financial might, identifying and empowering homegrown players has been an enormous part of their sustained success. Most of the Yankees' evaluators and coaches who discovered, advocated for and molded Schlittler and Rice probably don't care that the duo grew up in the shadow of Fenway.
Talent is talent, no matter where it comes from. If you can ball, you can ball.
And these guys most definitely ball.

Robinhood is broadening its offerings in a bid for more active traders who may be seeking trading access beyond traditional U.S. stock market hours.
The brokerage is expanding trading hours, adding crypto perpetuals and AI-powered automated trading tools to appeal to more active traders, it announced Tuesday evening at its HOOD Summit in Houston, Texas.
The new offerings reflect Robinhood's evolution beyond its commission-free stock-trading roots as it seeks to become a more comprehensive platform for active traders. The strategy puts the company increasingly in competition with both crypto-native platforms like Coinbase , which has expanded into derivatives and other financial products, and traditional brokerages like Schwab , which added 24/7 trading in select cryptocurrency futures on its thinkorswim platform this year.
As firms vie for customers who trade across a wider range of markets and hours, the competition among retail brokerages is moving beyond low trading costs toward access, speed and automation.
Robinhood shares jumped 3% in early trading Wednesday following the news.
"Ownership doesn't work without markets, and markets don't work without traders," Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev said in a statement. "We're making Robinhood the best place in the world for active traders by delivering tools once reserved for hedge funds, big banks, and quant firms."
Starting next year, Robinhood customers will be able to trade certain U.S. equities 24/7, including weekends. The move is an extension of its 24/5 trading feature, rolled out in 2023, that lets customers from Sunday at 8:00 PM ET to Friday at 8:00 PM ET.
Robinhood also introduced AI-powered automated trading tools that will let users build their own agents, following the launch of agentic trading earlier this year. The idea is that customers could use the agents to automate parts of the trading process, allowing them to pursue around-the-clock strategies.
Tenev noted that most markets went electronic about 20 years ago, and that although algorithms now driving much of the volume on exchanges, human traders' strategies still have a role.
"I don't think that's going to go away," he told CNBC's "Squawk Box" Wednesday. "I don't think it'll ever be 100% but it does open up a new capability frontier. Every time you have a new asset class – whether it be perps or earnings predictions or a new capability like AI tools – it creates a new domain where traders and market participants can compete, and my bet is there's lots of opportunities."
Additionally, the brokerage unveiled plans to allow users to trade crypto perpetual futures contracts in the Robinhood app, which offer leveraged exposure to cryptocurrencies without requiring traders to hold the underlying assets.

articles.title_orig: Tennessee set to execute a woman for the first time in two centuries
articles.title_zh: Tennessee set to execute a woman for the first time in two centuries
articles.content_orig:
Christa Pike, Tennessee's only female death row inmate , has lost her final appeal after the U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene in her imminent execution.
The nation's highest court denied Pike's request for a stay of execution on Sept. 29, less than 24 hours before Pike is set to be executed by lethal injection on Sept. 30. The court joins Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee and lower courts in rejecting arguments from Pike's attorneys that she should be spared because of her exceptionally traumatic childhood.
Also on Sept. 29, Amnesty International joined more than 100 women's advocacy groups and sex abuse experts in continuing to argue for a reprieve for Pike.
"It is unthinkable that Governor Lee would even consider moving forward with this execution," Justin Mazzola, deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA, said in a statement. "In this moment, people around the world are asking Governor Lee to grant clemency to Ms. Pike, and we add our voice to theirs."
Lee announced on Sept. 28 that he upheld Christa Pike's death sentence and was not planning to intervene in her execution. He did not provide an explanation.
If Pike's execution moves forward, she will become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years and only the 19th in the U.S. in the last 50 years. She was sentenced to death for the brutal and prolonged 1995 murder of her romantic rival, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer .
Pike's attorneys and more than 100 women's advocacy groups and sex abuse experts have been imploring the governor and courts to commute Pike's sentence to life in prison. They argued that Pike is so traumatized by repeated rapes throughout her girlhood, that the process of being executed by lethal injection will make her feel like she's being raped all over again.
They argue that amounts to cruel and unusual punishment in violation of the U.S. Constitution.
"She will relive the sounds, the smells, and the pain," wrote a dozen women's advocacy organizations in what's known as a friend-of-the court brief filed in the Tennessee Supreme Court on Sept. 10 and in the U.S. Supreme Court on Sept. 26. "She will feel it now as she did then. And it will be as horrific for her now as it was then."
While the Tennessee Attorney General's Office acknowledges that Pike had a childhood that involved repeated rapes, they have been arguing that her death sentence is a just punishment for her crime.
"Pike’s prior abuse and mental struggles are tragic to say the least," the state wrote in arguments to the Supreme Court this week. "But they are no cause to insulate her from a lawfully imposed and exhaustively reviewed death sentence that a jury of her peers imposed purely because of her own horrific conduct."
Here's what else you need to know about the case, including how Colleen Slemmer's mother feels more than 30 years after her daughter's murder.
On Jan. 12, 1995, 18-year-old Pike, her boyfriend, and another young woman lured Slemmer to the woods in Knoxville. Pike and her boyfriend, then-17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp, tortured and murdered Slemmer in a crime that made international headlines both for its brutality and because of Pike's gender and youth.
"Armed with a box cutter and meat cleaver, Pike and two accomplices lured Slemmer to an isolated area. There, Pike kneed Slemmer’s head, threw her to the ground, and repeatedly kicked her," the Tennessee Attorney General's Office wrote in court documents. "When Slemmer tried to flee, Pike sliced her stomach with the box cutter. ... As Slemmer begged for her life, Pike repeatedly kicked her in the face. Pike then cut Slemmer’s throat as she begged for mercy."
After Slemmer made one final attempt to escape, Pike smashed the back of her head with a rock, they wrote. Shipp also carved a pentagram into Slemmer's chest, and Pike later showed off a piece of Slemmer's skull to a friend.
Pike was sentenced to death and Shipp got a life sentence because at 17, he wasn't eligible for the death penalty.
For Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, Pike's execution more than 30 years after her daughter's murder represents long-awaited justice.
"I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting," Martinez told WBIR-TV in 2021. "There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was."
Martinez recently told WBIR-TV that she plans to attend Pike's execution this week.
"I'll hold Colleen's picture up to remind her of what she did," Martinez told the station. "She never apologized − never even tried − or her family."
She said she remembers her daughter as a playful and compassionate young woman who loved roller skating, computers, and playing old games with her family. She laments that her daughter has been so overshadowed by Pike over the years.
"It's never about the victims," she said. "It's like Colleen was never there."
Court records show that Pike became a rape victim before she was even in preschool. Her grandmother's boyfriend targeted her for years, sexually assaulting her until she was in kindergarten, according to court documents obtained by USA TODAY.
At the age of 11, a neighbor raped Pike in an attack that caused an infection and preceded a suicide attempt at the age of 12. And at 17, a stranger attacked Pike while she was out walking, forced her into the woods, and raped her, court records say.
Pike's execution is certain to take her back to that trauma, the women's advocacy organizations wrote in the friend-of-the-court brief. The experience, which involves being strapped down, is likely to be so visceral to Pike, that it will be unconstitutionally cruel, they argue.
"There is a substantial risk she will feel and believe that she is being raped to death," argue the groups, which include the Coalition Against Trafficking in Women , Rights4Girls and Survivors Justice Project.
The groups, joined by dozens more sex assault experts and women's advocates, also appealed directly to Lee and urged him to commute Pike's sentence to life in prison.
"It is not just that she was a toddler when she was sexually abused for the first time, or that she was raped by three more men before her 18th birthday," they wrote in a letter to Lee on Sept. 10. "It is that Christa was forced to cope with her sexual abuse and rape virtually alone, without any of the victim support services that we know are so vital to recovery."
During a recent three-day hearing in a Knoxville courtroom, prosecutors said they would try to keep men away from Pike during the two-week period known as death watch, when guards closely monitor inmates in part to prevent them from dying by suicide.
David Wickenheiser, an assistant attorney general, quoted from a psychologist's report at the hearing that though "Christa will always carry that history of trauma with her ... she now has the tools and emotions to deal with life stressors."
Senior Judge Mark Ward, the special master appointed by the Tennessee Supreme Court who presided over the hearing, concluded that the Tennessee Department of Corrections has "minimized the potential" for Pike to experience significant triggering and that mental suffering alone is not enough to violate the Constitution's protections against cruel and unusual punishment.
Pike's attorneys requested a stay of execution in the Supreme Court on Sept. 25, arguing that it was an open question whether mental suffering during an execution can be considered a constitutional violation.
"This case presents uniquely compelling circumstances where this Court is likely to consider such an important constitutional question," they wrote. "While the public may have an interest in seeing judgments carried out, it also has an interest that its citizens not be tortured to death in the name of the people."
The court denied the stay without issuing a written opinion.

articles.content_orig:
HOUSTON -- Sam Antonacci tripped while running out of the dugout during pregame introductions for Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series between his White Sox and the Astros on Tuesday at Daikin Park.
That misstep was pretty much the only one encountered by Chicago during a 6-3 victory over the American League West champions. With another win on Wednesday or Thursday, the White Sox would claim their first playoff series victory since a four-game sweep of the Astros in the 2005 World Series, with staff ace Sean Burke set to start against Hunter Brown, Houston’s No. 1, on Wednesday.
A victory in either of these next two days would send the White Sox to Cleveland for a best-of-five AL Division Series. The Guardians won the AL Central by one game, despite the White Sox winning the season series, 7-6.
In the history of the best-of-three Wild Card Series, teams taking a 1-0 lead have gone on to win the series 21 of 24 times (88%), including 17 two-game sweeps. Visiting teams have won 12 of 15 series (80%) in which they have gone ahead 1-0, including nine sweeps. However, the most recent rally by a home team that lost Game 1 happened just last year, when the Yankees came back against the Red Sox.
But anyone who has followed Chicago this season understands the White Sox aren't going to get ahead of themselves.
“Our mindset is we’re taking it as though we’re 0-0,” Antonacci said. “A lot can happen, and they have really good arms. We're trying to win each pitch, and hopefully, that will help us win each inning and ultimately win the ball game. Just trying to compete at a high level every game.”
“We can’t be thinking about the end of the game tomorrow,” catcher Kyle Teel said. “It’s just an inning at a time, a pitch at a time, and I feel that’s the way to be successful.”
Tuesday was a bullpen game for both teams: by choice for the White Sox, and more out of necessity for the Astros. Houston used their main starters against the A’s over the weekend to win the AL West, which they needed to do to lock in a playoff spot.
The strategy worked much better for the visiting South Siders on Tuesday.

Rookie Hagen Smith pitched three scoreless innings, allowing only two hits. He struck out one but used his four-pitch mix to record seven swings and misses, according to Statcast. He retired Yordan Alvarez with two outs and a runner on third to end the third inning. Alvarez, a frontrunner for the AL Most Valuable Player Award, is 4-for-23 with one extra-base hit against the White Sox this season.
“Really, really good. Attacking the zone,” Teel said of Smith. “You could tell he wanted the ball.”
“Kyle did a great job game-planning for me, and [I trusted] him back there,” Smith said. “Just kind of attacking it with everything. A lot of cutters and sliders and just kind of attacking with those a lot early, and heaters here and there.”
Meanwhile, opener AJ Blubaugh could not find the zone for Houston, throwing just 13 of his 27 pitches for strikes. The Astros needed two pitchers to get through the first inning, although they combined to allow just one unearned run.
Colson Montgomery hit ninth for the first time this season, two days after talking about using the playoffs as a reset after setting MLB's single-season record with 227 strikeouts. That reset was real, as Montgomery launched a Statcast-projected 432-foot home run in the fourth off Miguel Ullola.
“He had a good fastball, so I had to be ready,” Montgomery said. “I felt ready. I felt on time with everything, and just the last pitch, I was probably more committed to what I was trying to do. Two strikes, you kind of lock in a little bit more.”
Four pitchers took the mound after Smith, with Sean Newcomb yielding Nelson Velázquez’s two-run pinch-hit blast in the fifth. David Sandlin worked 1 1/3 innings before giving way to Grant Taylor.
Taylor threw a career-high 54 pitches , covering 2 1/3 innings with five strikeouts. One of those strikeouts came to end the eighth, when Yainer Diaz took a called third strike on a 3-2 curve.
Braden Montgomery added two hits and scored once, as did Chase Meidroth. As for Antonacci? He drove home two with a single after scoring the game’s first run and also got hit by a pitch in the sixth. He set the single-season franchise mark with 27 HBP in 2026, so it only makes sense.
Let’s go back to that original dugout trip involving Antonacci. The White Sox have had plenty of fun while winning this season, sometimes to excess. So naturally, Antonacci later claimed the stumble was staged.
“There may have been some money involved. Just like I may have been Spider-Man,” said a smiling Antonacci, referring to a rumor that he went to see Spider-Man: Brand New Day with Miguel Vargas, dressed as the superhero . “We’ll never know.”
“That’s the word on the street,” Taylor said of Antonacci’s stumble. “It looked a little too real.”

The Trump administration is rolling back federal fuel-economy standards for new vehicles. American automakers will now be required to improve the efficiency of their fleets by up to 1% a year, aiming for an average of 34.9 miles per gallon by 2031 — down from the Biden-era target of 50.4 mpg.

New York prosecutors are reopening a 2024 alleged rape case involving Cornell University students. A woman identified as Jane Doe says in a new lawsuit that multiple men drugged and raped her at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. Cornell has defended its response , saying it conducted a months-long Title IX investigation. No criminal charges were filed at the time.
Five British men have been released on bail after being detained near a military base for alleged terror offenses. The British base is used by the U.S. military for strikes on Iran. President Trump has questioned why the men were released.
Turkey is positioning itself for a bigger role in the Middle East as questions grow about the U.S. security footprint in the region. Ankara is expanding its military and political reach, but economic pressures and rising tensions with Israel could limit those ambitions. Syria has also become a key test, with Turkey playing a growing role in reconstruction and security as Israel pushes back against its expanding influence.

Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich became the story when Russia arrested him on espionage charges while he was reporting. He spent 16 months in prison before being convicted and released in a prisoner swap . Gershkovich tells NPR's Leila Fadel that he turned to what he knew: listening, observing and writing. His prison journals became the backbone of his memoir, This Cursed Beautiful Land: A Russian-American Story . He also reflects on the strange reversal of being a journalist accustomed to observing others — and suddenly becoming the person everyone was watching. Listen to the full interview here .
by Peter O'Dowd , Here & Now 's host-correspondent
A large piece of ice that broke off the Mendenhall glacier in Juneau, Alaska. Peter O'Dowd/Here & Now hide caption
A flood happens like clockwork every summer in Juneau, Alaska.
When the weather warms up, a reservoir in the mountains above the city fills with billions of gallons of melted ice and eventually breaks past the glacial dam holding it back.
Even though I'm based in Arizona, I've been watching from afar every year since 2023, when the glacial outburst flood ripped houses into the raging Mendenhall River. The story is personal. My in-laws are from Juneau, and they live in the floodzone.
That's why it felt like it was time to bring Here & Now 's climate-solutions project, Reverse Course , to the last frontier. While climate change is threatening lives and livelihoods around the globe, no state in the country has warmed faster than Alaska.
Along with fellow climate journalist Chris Bentley, we boarded small planes, ferries and helicopters to get a close-up view of the risks facing the state. Chris met people from the Chilkat Indian Village in Klukwan who are working to create a warning system for landslides triggered by heavy rain; and I spoke with Juneau residents racing to protect the city from glacial floods that are likely to last another 20 years, or more.
Thankfully, this summer, my in-law's house and the rest of Juneau stayed dry.
But about two weeks after we left town, a landslide triggered by a collapsing glacier ripped through mountain villages in Nepal and Tibet. While the scale of the devastation was beyond anything experienced in Alaska, the underlying truth remains: A warming planet is destabilizing ice sheets around the world. The hazards are getting closer to home.

articles.title_orig: North Korea denies planting mines that injured 3 South Korean soldiers, accuses Seoul of conspiracy
articles.title_zh: North Korea denies planting mines that injured 3 South Korean soldiers, accuses Seoul of conspiracy
articles.content_orig:
Blast during search operation near border fuels political tensions amid attempts to revive diplomatic channels
South Korea has demanded an apology from North Korea over a landmine blast that injured three soldiers, saying they were hurt by North Korean mines on the southern side of the border.
Kang Hyun-woo, the director of operations at South Korea’s joint chiefs of staff, demanded an apology and “responsible measures” from Pyongyang over the blast, which occurred on 21 September during a search operation south of the border.
He also called for an immediate halt to North Korea’s mine-laying and border fortification, which he said violated the armistice and the spirit of inter-Korean agreements. North Korea would bear “all responsibility” for any future developments, he said.
The incident echoes a 2015 mine blast in the demilitarised zone between the countries that seriously injured two South Korean soldiers and prompted Seoul to resume propaganda broadcasts over loudspeakers. North Korea responded to the move with artillery fire across the border before expressing regret during high-level talks .
The US-led UN command (UNC), which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war, said on Wednesday that a joint investigation with South Korea’s military had identified a live North Korean anti-personnel mine on the southern side of the military demarcation line (MDL), the de facto border.
The UNC said an armistice violation had occurred and that it was addressing the issue through “established armistice mechanisms”.
The explosions occurred about 10 metres south of the MDL on the western front, as troops searched an area where North Korea was suspected of laying mines.
Two blasts went off about a minute apart, seriously injuring a battalion commander, whose foot was reportedly severed at the ankle, and an engineer. A third officer was present and has minor injuries from the explosion.
On Monday, South Korea’s military said interim findings showed the blasts were “highly likely” to have been caused by North Korean mines
North Korea has denied involvement. In a statement carried by state media on Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong-un , called the incident “an obvious self-staged farce”.
“Our soldiers have never once crossed the border,” she said, warning that if South Korean troops fired directly at North Korean soldiers, border units would carry out “immediate and merciless retaliation”.
Chris Green, a senior consultant at the International Crisis Group, said the investigation findings would not settle the matter politically because the North would always have “guaranteed plausible deniability”.
There are no working communication channels between the two Koreas. Pyongyang severed ties in 2024, declared South Korea a hostile state and has since laid mines and built fortifications along the border. “Accidental escalation on the Korean peninsula is always just a few steps away and it’s fewer steps now than it was in 2015,” Green said.
The blast presents a challenge for South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung , who has sought to revive diplomacy with Pyongyang. Last week, he told the UN general assembly that Seoul would be a “pacemaker” for peace, and urged Washington to ease sanctions in exchange for a freeze on North Korea’s weapons programmes.
The incident has also fuelled political tensions at home. Opposition politicians questioned whether the investigation had been delayed to avoid overshadowing Lee’s UN speech, a suggestion the presidential office denied.
The conservative People Power party has also called for the return of the propaganda loudspeakers, which were switched off and dismantled under Lee last year.
The mine blast adds to other diplomatic difficulties facing Lee. On Monday, Seoul demanded an apology from Ukraine after its president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, disclosed the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
Seoul said the two sides had agreed to keep the transfer secret, citing the men’s safety and diplomatic and security considerations. Some critics said the secrecy was about not upsetting Pyongyang.

articles.title_orig: Restaurant named after Xi Jinping attacked by Chinese nationals in South Korea
articles.title_zh: Restaurant named after Xi Jinping attacked by Chinese nationals in South Korea
articles.content_orig:
Surveillance footage show a group of masked men spraying lacquer across the restaurant in South Korea's Seongnam
A restaurant in South Korea named after Chinese leader Xi Jinping has been vandalised by a group of Chinese nationals who fled home right after the attack, police say.
Surveillance footage from the restaurant in Seongnam, a city south of Seoul, shows four masked men storming the premises in the early hours of 24 September, smashing furniture and spraying lacquer.
The restaurant's owner told local media he picked the name Xi Jinping because he "wanted it to be the best Chinese restaurant [in South Korea]". He added that "There was no political intent".
The restaurant has been running for eight years but only began getting demands for a name change over the past year, The Chosun Daily reported.
The owner said that in August last year, when news broke that Xi would be attending the Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation Summit in South Korea, he received dozens of phone calls relating to these demands. Some people even offered money, he said.
"People claiming to run businesses in China proposed large sums if we changed the name," he told The Chosun Daily. "They were persistent."
In April this year, someone filed a complaint with South Korea's Ministry of Intellectual Property regarding a dish on the restaurant's menu called Xi Jinping Special Rice, but the ministry eventually closed the case, finding no issues.
The owner said last week's attack was the largest one he's experienced over the past year, telling local media the property damage amounted to about 15 million won ($11,100; Â£8,400).
Xi Jinping restaurant closed for five days following the attack and reopened on Tuesday. The owner says his team is now considering a new name for the eatery.
Police on Tuesday said the four suspects were Chinese men between the ages of 20 and 40. After the attack they are believed to have fled to Shanghai and Yantai, a city in China's Shandong province.
Police say they are planning to request red notices from Interpol for the four men. These are not arrest warrants, but rather requests to police around the world to detain someone pending extradition.
Xi Jinping restaurant serves a wide range of Chinese dishes, although its menu also includes some South Korean offerings, according to screenshots shared online. Google reviewers have given it an average score of four out of five stars.

Two North Korean soldiers captured fighting for Russia against Ukraine are now in South Korea.
The move has raised questions ​over how they will be investigated, protected and resettled, and the legal basis for their transfer.
The soldiers are expected to undergo questioning and security screening before the South Korean authorities decide whether to grant them protection and begin the resettlement process.
Seoul 's Unification Ministry said on Monday their cases would be reviewed under relevant laws and past practices, suggesting that the North Korean Defectors Protection and Settlement ⁠Support Act would apply.
Under the law, the National Intelligence Service (NIS) investigates applicants in temporary protective custody, verifying their identities, reasons for leaving North Korea and security-related matters.
The investigation and temporary protection may last up to 90 days, with a possible extension in unavoidable circumstances.
The soldiers’ military backgrounds and firsthand knowledge of North Korea’s deployment to Russia could result in more extensive debriefing.
Those granted protection usually receive resettlement training before entering South Korean society.
Yu Yong-weon, an opposition lawmaker who met the soldiers in Ukraine in February 2025, said they had served in North Korean special forces and ⁠could provide information on Pyongyang 's training, military capabilities and participation in the war.
The unification minister normally determines whether a North Korean arrival qualifies for protection, although the NIS director can make the decision on national security grounds.
Yu told Reuters the sensitivity of the case could also keep them out of public view longer than other North Korean arrivals.
Their physical and ⁠psychological condition is also likely to be assessed.
Yu said when he met them they were being held separately at a Ukrainian detention facility and the ​prolonged isolation and uncertainty ⁠may have affected their mental health.
The Third Geneva Convention requires prisoners of war to be released and repatriated without delay after active hostilities end. That does not necessarily prohibit earlier release or transfer to a third country.
South Korea and Ukraine have not disclosed the legal basis for their transfer, including whether it formally ends the soldiers’ POW status.
Peter ‌Ward, a research fellow at the Sejong Institute, said repatriation was a basic principle governing POWs ‌but should not apply where it could damage their welfare or human rights.
"There is ample basis under humanitarian and human rights law for these POWs to be transferred to a third country of their choice so long as that third country of their choice is prepared to take them," Ward said.
Lee Shin-wha, a Korea University professor and former envoy for North Korean human rights, said the transfer could still generate legal and ⁠diplomatic friction because international law treats North Korea as a separate state, while South Korea considers North Koreans as its citizens.
Their stated wish to come to the South and the risks they could face in the North provide grounds for accepting them, she said.
International human rights law would weigh against returning the soldiers if they faced a real risk of torture, persecution or other serious mistreatment.
The principle of non-refoulement prohibits sending people to a country where they face such risks.
Lee said repatriation was the general rule for POWs, but international practice also recognised voluntary repatriation and barred returns that could lead to persecution or torture.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has praised soldiers who committed suicide while fighting against Ukrainian forces in Russia's Kursk region where the pair were captured.
The two men repeatedly ‌expressed a desire to go to South Korea, including in media interviews and during a meeting with Yu.
Ward said North Korea had little basis ​under international law to demand their return.
South Korea, which is a major arms producer, has ‌faced pressure from some Western countries and Kyiv to provide Ukraine with lethal ⁠weapons but has so far focused on non-lethal aid including demining equipment.
President Lee Jae Myung announced a $100 million support package for Ukraine at a NATO ⁠summit in July, while his government reiterated that lethal weapons were excluded. Seoul also pledged continued humanitarian assistance and support for reconstruction.
At their July summit, Lee and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy agreed that the North Korean ‌POW issue should be handled in accordance with the ​soldiers’ free will, international law and humanitarian principles.
South Korea ‌demanded an apology from Ukraine after Zelenskiy disclosed the transfer at the ​UN General Assembly last week, saying Kyiv had breached an agreement to keep it confidential.
Seoul said confidentiality was necessary to protect the soldiers and relatives in North Korea.
Kyiv has said no secrecy agreement existed.
