articles.title_orig: Three takeaways from Trump's 'Super Intelligence' summit
articles.title_zh: Three takeaways from Trump's 'Super Intelligence' summit
articles.content_orig:
Trump met top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday to discuss AI
US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses on Tuesday for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the minds that are "building America's Golden Age".
The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry.
The meeting came as some tech executives and experts have called for tighter oversight of AI, citing concerns about the potential risks it poses to humanity.
Here are three key takeaways from Trump's tech summit at the White House.
Trump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting.
The president said the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.
Under the agreement, which Trump posted online , external , the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.
The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues.
They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways."
The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said.
"And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president."
Trump with top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday
Trump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board.
Zuckerberg said the accord gives the "American people and customers the confidence that the technology works" as intended, calling the meeting a "historic conversation".
Amodei called it a way "to win safely", referring to the president's comment earlier this month that "whoever wins AI, wins".
But not all technology experts are impressed with the accord.
Nanyang Technological University AI governance researcher Jose Miguelito Enriquez said the pact shows "emerging consensus" but does not address whether AI developers should be held accountable for incidents.
It is "deeply unimpressive" and comes despite calls from some world leaders and industry figures for tighter regulations around the technology, said law professor Kimberlee Weatherall from the University of Sydney.
The agreement appears to allow firms to "define what counts as safety" and does not state what consequences there are for any breaches, Weatherall said.
"The accord should be ignored, for the distraction it is," she added.
Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings
Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they?
Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks in response to calls from some industry figures for tighter oversight over the technology.
On Monday, OpenAI said it had scrapped the release of its latest flagship AI model , GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns.
The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after high-profile incidents involving its technology, including its models accessing Australian government platforms without authorisation .
Jeannie Paterson from the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Ethics at the University of Melbourne said self-regulation could mean that companies set "only minimal safeguards".
The agreement inspires "very little confidence" as recent incidents of AI going rogue suggest companies have been undisciplined in their approach, she added.
Trump also reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centres - the crucial computing infrastructure that powers AI.
The rollout of data centres has drawn pushback around the US over concerns about electricity usage and their potential impact on communities.
Data centre construction has also emerged as a potential political obstacle for Trump's Republican party ahead of the US midterm elections in November.
A survey conducted by Marist Poll in partnership with NPR and PBS News , external earlier this month found that 65% of registered voters opposed data centres being built in their areas.
Responding to those concerns, Trump said tech companies would work to make people "happy" about the construction of data centres.
"These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities," Trump told reporters.
The president previously said on social media that the only reason communities should oppose data centres is if they "want to end up being backwards and poor".
Huang, whose company produces computer chips essential for running AI, said after the meeting that data centres should be called "super intelligence factories".
These facilities are "reindustrialising the United States", creating jobs across the economy, he added.
Also on Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence.
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.
"As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence," the order said.
Trump spoke to the media alongside tech executives after the summit
During an address to the United Nations General Assembly last week , Trump said the word "artificial" made the technology "sound fake".
Some tech leaders, including Zuckerberg and Musk, and other people close to the president have already started to use the term.
With tech leaders adopting the term, the US "may well be able to set the nomenclature," Paterson said.
But some experts said after Trump's UN speech that they thought the term was unlikely to gain widespread traction because it is a name typically used to refer to more advanced systems.

By ALESIA FIDDLER - TRAVEL REPORTER
Published: 01:30 EDT, 30 September 2026 | Updated: 03:39 EDT, 30 September 2026
With undisrupted coastal views, clear skies and a beautiful white-washed church, it would be easy to mistake this small island for a piece of Italy .
Lamb Holm, however, is actually part of the Orkney Islands in Scotland - thousands of miles away from the b el paese .
Now completely uninhabited, the remote island has an intriguing history and was used to house prisoners of war (POW) during the Second World War .
Alongside its beautiful beach, Lamb Holm has a more direct link to Italy – many of the POWs brought there were Italian, according to National Churches Trust .
Captured in North Africa, over 1,000 prisoners were taken to Orkney to help build the Churchill Barriers that now serve as causeways for the Orkney Islands.
The Italian prisoners were based on Lamb Holm and put to work in the quarries or construction.
Holm Lamb, part of the Orkney Islands, has an intriguing history linking it back to Italy
Aside from its beautiful coastal views, the island is also home to an Italian chapel
It was built by Italian prisoners of war during World War II and still stands today
During this period, the men were provided with two unused huts to repurpose into a chapel. The Italians got to work at once, transforming the space into the beautiful white building that stands today.
Artist Domenico Chiocchetti was among those captured and taken to the island. Wanting to celebrate Italy's beauty and culture, he painted the Madonna of the Olive Branch above the altar inside the chapel.
The overall construction of the site was a team effort amongst the prisoners, with electricians, cement workers and a blacksmith all pooling together to transform the corrugated iron of the huts.
There are two beautiful stained-glass windows of St Francis of Assisi and St Catherine of Siena.
Indeed, from the front of the building, it is almost impossible to tell the origins of the chapel - it could easily be mistaken for one straight from the Italian countryside.
At the end of the war, the prisoners left the island - but some returned later on to revisit the chapel they had built, according to Daily Record .
A declaration was signed in 1996 between Orkney and Moena, Domenico Chiocchetti's hometown, formally tying the two places together.
And despite being part of the UK, it is considerably more tricky to reach Lamb Holm than it is Italy - which is a short two-hour Ryanair hop away from London.
Visitors can either get a ferry from mainland Scotland to Kirkwall and then drive or get a bus to Lamb Holm.
Inside, the chapel was beautifully painted by prisoner and artist Domenio Chiocchetti
Alternatively, it's possible to fly with Loganair from mainland spots such as Aberdeen from £114 each way in October.
The flight takes a swift 55 minutes, followed by a 13-minute drive to Lamb Holm.
It's worth noting for visitors, though, that the island is mostly empty; there isn't all that much to do aside from visit the chapel and enjoy the landscape.
However, just a three-minute walk from the church is a coastal spot called Italian Beach, which boasts a beautiful sandy shore backed by rocks.
Nearby, visitors can find the Orkney Wine Company and a rum and spirit store.
There is also the Oyster Restoration Company which aims to rebuild and restore oyster reefs.

The footage appears to show authorities chasing Wilber Rafael Garces Perez just before he was shot (Credit: X @Savsays via X).
A Venezuelan national who was shot by an ICE officer following a vehicle pursuit in Austin earlier this month has been charged with assaulting, resisting, interfering with and impeding a federal officer, the Justice Department announced Tuesday.
Federal prosecutors allege that Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez, 28, refused ICE officers' commands to exit his vehicle during a targeted traffic stop before speeding away and striking one officer in the torso with his driver's side-view mirror.
Garces-Perez faces up to 20 years in federal prison if convicted, according to DOJ.
According to the complaint, officers first spotted Garces-Perez's vehicle outside a restaurant, ran its license plate and confirmed that an immigration judge had issued a final order of removal against him before initiating the stop.
AUSTIN ICE SHOOTING SPARKS FIGHT OVER VENEZUELAN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT'S DEPORTATION
A federal complaint states that one ICE officer turned off his body camera during a vehicle pursuit that later ended with a second officer shooting Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez. (Department of Justice)
The accounts differ over whether the vehicles made contact as officers stopped Garces-Perez. The officer told investigators there was no contact between the vehicles, while Garces-Perez claimed the ICE SUV's maneuver caused a collision before the officers approached him.
During the encounter, Garces-Perez provided officers with his driver's license, according to the complaint.
The officers described the initial encounter as "pleasant and not aggressive," according to the complaint. After officers instructed Garces-Perez to place the vehicle in park and step out, body camera footage shows him abruptly closing his window and driving away, according to the complaint.
EXCLUSIVE: DHS SECRETARY MULLIN SLAMS SANCTUARY POLITICIANS AS ATTACKS ON ICE OFFICERS SKYROCKET
Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez, 28, was shot as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers were trying to take him into custody in Austin, Texas. (Austin Police Department)
Garces-Perez later told federal investigators that he disregarded the officers' command to exit the vehicle and drove away, according to the complaint. The complaint states that he was read his Miranda rights in Spanish, said he understood them and agreed to speak with investigators without an attorney present.
As he drove away, Garces-Perez's driver's side-view mirror struck one of the officers in the torso, according to the complaint.
According to the complaint, ICE officers pursued Garces-Perez through commercial and residential areas with emergency lights and sirens activated.
The officer wearing a body camera lost sight of both Garces-Perez and the second ICE officer while requesting assistance from a DPS dispatcher and then turned off his camera, according to the complaint. The second officer, who later fired his weapon, was not equipped with a body camera .
DEM REACTIONS WITHIN MOMENTS OF AUSTIN ICE SHOOTING SPARK VIRAL OUTRAGE LOCALLY, ONLINE: 'DISQUALIFYING'
Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez, 28, was charged with assaulting, resisting, interfering with and impeding a federal officer following an ICE vehicle pursuit in Austin, Texas, according to the Justice Department. (Wilber Garces / Facebook)
The second officer later called his partner and reported that Garces-Perez had attempted to strike him with his vehicle, prompting the officer to fire his service weapon, according to the complaint.
Garces-Perez was struck by a bullet in his upper back, according to the complaint. He told investigators that the officer's SUV rammed his vehicle to force it into a spinout and that, after he was shot, the officer opened his driver's door, removed the keys from the ignition and told him to remain inside while an ambulance was en route.
Garces-Perez's immigration case has also been the subject of competing claims.
Fox News previously reported that his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said the order was issued after a hearing notice was sent to an old address despite Garces-Perez having updated his address with the court.
TRUMP REVIVES SUPREME COURT IMMIGRATION SHOWDOWN AFTER HOCHUL PARDON TORPEDOED FIRST CASE
Federal prosecutors allege Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez fled a targeted ICE traffic stop in Austin before his vehicle's side mirror struck an officer in the torso. (Department of Justice)
ICE has disputed claims surrounding his immigration status, saying his work authorization expired in 2025 and that a work permit does not itself confer lawful immigration status.
His attorney has said Garces-Perez remains seriously ill and has a bullet lodged in his body while being held at an ICE detention facility .
Lincoln-Goldfinch, responding to the criminal complaint in a social media post, called for DHS to release the body camera footage .
"The criminal complaint also provides another critical piece of information: one of the officers involved in the incident had a body camera that was turned off at some point during the pursuit. We have not seen that footage. DHS must release the body camera footage immediately and provide full transparency to the American public," Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote.
"He is now facing proceedings in both a federal criminal case and his federal immigration habeas case. We are working through what these developments mean, and we will share additional information as we are able."
DOJ said Garces-Perez made his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday.

articles.title_zh: S Korea demands apology from Pyongyang over landmine blast
articles.content_orig:
Explosions in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) earlier this month have set off a war of words between North and South Korea
South Korea's military has demanded an apology from North Korea for landmine blasts along their shared border that wounded South Korean soldiers earlier this month.
Three South Korean personnel were injured by explosions in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) - a buffer zone separating the two Koreas, on 21 September.
South Korea said on Tuesday it was "certain" that the blasts, which happened on South Korea's side of the DMZ, came from North Korean mines. It vowed to take "corresponding measures" for what he said was a violation of a decades-old armistice.
North Korea has denied responsibility for the blasts, calling Seoul's claims "groundless" and a "farce" to escalate tensions on the peninsula.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, accused South Korea of "cooking up" the claims for "political and military provocation".
Kim denied suggestions that North Korean had crossed the border to plant the mines, calling it "a deliberate and planned strained assertion to shift the responsibility for escalating tension" to North Korea.
Her statement, published in state media on Wednesday, also warned the South to be "prepared for paying price for the farce of their own making."
South Korea says the mines are believed to have been laid by Pyongyang to fortify its border. In a statement on Wednesday, it called for North Korea to apologise for the blast and put an immediate stop to such fortification activities along the border.
South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul previously said on Tuesday that the blasts were a "clear" violation of the 1953 armistice, which halted active combat in the Korean War.
That armistice resulted in the creation of the 4km-wide (2.5-mile) DMZ, a buffer strip containing the Military Demarcation Line which marks the land border between the two Koreas.
In the decades since, sporadic clashes and mine explosions have broken out in the DMZ.
In 2015, two South Korean soldiers were maimed by landmines while patrolling the area. South Korea said the mines had been secretly planted by North Korean soldiers near a South Korean guard post - a claim that Pyongyang denied.
Kim referenced that 2015 incident in her statement on Wednesday, claiming South Korea had used that as a "pretext" to escalate tensions, and were doing the same thing now.
Ties between Pyongyang and Seoul have only deteriorated since 2015, raising the risk of friction when such incidents happen.
Christopher Green, a senior consultant with Crisis Group, tells the BBC that "The North Koreans have been wilfully attempting to harden the border [and] eliminate inter-Korean relations".
As a result, he adds, the two Koreas no longer have the "same low-level communication" that they shared in 2015.
"Accidental escalation on the Korean Peninsula is always just a few steps away, and it's fewer steps now than it was in 2015," he says.
The United Nations Command, which conducted the on-site investigations into the blasts with the South Korean military, said it would handle the violation of the 1953 armistice "through established Armistice mechanisms".
"UNC remains committed to maintaining and enforcing the Armistice Agreement and fulfilling its responsibilities to preserve stability and prevent escalation on the Korean Peninsula," it said.

articles.title_orig: Apple Will Sell 6 Million iPhone Duos in 2026, Counterpoint Says
articles.title_zh: Apple Will Sell 6 Million iPhone Duos in 2026, Counterpoint Says
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
The iPhone Duo ‘s launch has sparked a duality of opinion: Is it worth upgrading to Apple’s new foldable phone?
The conversation around the $1,999 device, which becomes available Oct. 23 , is everywhere – and not just in the comments of my Instagram Reels showing the new phone in action . Commentaries and social posts about the headline-grabbing device abound. And despite Android foldables having been around for years, I’ve received more questions about the iPhone Duo than any other foldable. Even CNET’s own reporters are divided on whether it’s worth buying .
I’m holding off on forming a final opinion until I’ve had a chance to properly test the iPhone Duo . My limited time with the phone at Apple Park simply isn’t enough to make a definitive call. What I can say with some certainty, though, is that Apple isn’t expecting everyone to rush out and buy its flashy new handset.
Foldables have been a niche category since their inception, and they’re likely to remain one even with Apple’s entry into the market. Globally, cumulative foldable phone shipments in the eight years since the category launched are slated to surpass 100 million units by the end of 2026, according to Counterpoint Research. That’s a significant number, but also just a fraction of the billions of phones sold in that period, including a projected 1.07 billion total smartphone shipments this year alone.
For many consumers, the biggest deterrent is the price. The passport-size Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 , for example, starts at $1,900, while the more traditional book-style Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Motorola Razr Fold fall in the same price range. There are more affordable options, such as the clamshell-style Motorola Razr , but even that starts at a not-insignificant $800. Many people may struggle to understand why they need a foldable phone when their (less expensive) slab phone does the trick just fine.
Apple is likely aware of this, which is why the iPhone Duo exists as an option rather than a replacement for any of the company’s existing models. Its release alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max signals that the Duo is positioned as an ultra-premium device for those who want something fresh – and who have the money to spare. Reports suggesting the iPhone Duo will be available in limited quantities reinforce its place as a status symbol for Apple’s biggest fans who are willing to branch out.
“I don’t think the brands want to make [foldable phones] mainstream in terms of volume,” says Nabila Popal, senior research director at IDC. “It’s a very intentional portfolio strategy to have different devices cater to different demographics, and I think that’s what Apple has really achieved with this launch.”
As unique and distinctive as foldable phones are to use, they don’t offer much of a selling point to most people. Despite rampant complaints about smartphones being too predictable and boring, people also tend to like what’s familiar and, more importantly, what already works well for their needs. Traditional smartphones – even more budget-friendly options – have optimized just about every element from cameras to battery life to display quality.
Still, foldable phones are a breath of fresh air in such a stagnant industry. Their versatile design is ideal for consuming vertical and horizontal content, as well as for multitasking. They’re also quite a statement piece at any gathering, eliciting curious glances and inquiries from fascinated onlookers.
Before the iPhone Duo’s release, 75% of adults said they were uninterested in a foldable iPhone , according to a CNET survey. Now that the phone has debuted, those numbers could quickly change.
In fact, analysts predict the iPhone Duo could give the overall foldables market a significant boost. IDC forecasts that global foldable shipments will grow by more than 12% this year, with Apple’s entry driving much of that growth. The research firm also expects that Apple will ship more than 17 million foldable iPhones by 2027, giving the company a nearly 40% global market share by the end of next year.
“The category will remain niche, but it will gain popularity and visibility,” Popal says.
Despite growing interest, the high price will keep many shoppers at bay, she notes. But for consumers who have wanted a foldable phone without giving up Apple’s iOS – and who have therefore disregarded the range of Android options – the Duo could be particularly appealing.
Despite Apple’s late entry into the foldable phone market, unique touches could help the Duo stand out from even the most well-established players, such as Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold series.
One example of how Apple’s hardware and software expertise could elevate the foldable experience is the seamless way content moves from the Duo’s cover display to the inner screen as soon as you open the phone. That cascading effect highlights Apple’s ability to optimize the interface across both screens, making the transition feel fluid and visually striking.
The matte inner display adds another layer of polish. It reduces reflections and makes the crease less noticeable, while giving the screen a more refined feel. And while the Duo can only run two apps side by side, setting up a multitasking layout is much easier than on competing Android foldables, where the process can often feel finicky.
“Those touches are what make the Duo stand out and feel extremely premium; it’s just a good experience,” Popal says. “Apple is great at making you want something that you didn’t know [you wanted] before.”
Perhaps that advantage could pressure competitors to improve their software and elevate the foldable experience on their own devices. Apps like Instagram, for example, still aren’t always optimized for the wider inner displays of foldable phones, though passport-style foldables like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 do a better job of accommodating vertical content in portrait orientation. And while developers on the Android side have to contend with a range of devices as well as form factors (clamshell, book-style, passport-size, etc.), Apple has one foldable experience they can really work to perfect.
While some detractors say they’d prefer a flip-style iPhone to the Duo’s compact book-style design, Carolina Milanesi, president and principal analyst at Creative Strategies, argues that the Duo’s more versatile build and 1.4:1 aspect ratio give it greater practical appeal, especially for entertainment.
Similar to the Galaxy Z Fold 8, it feels intuitive to flip the Duo to portrait orientation when viewing vertical content on the 7.6-inch inner screen, then revert to landscape for horizontal videos. The 5.4-inch cover screen on the Duo is also more functional and spacious than a flip phone’s.
“When you hold it, it feels familiar because you have so many other analog objects that are kind of the same [size], whether it’s a Moleskine [notebook] or your passport,” Milanesi adds.
Plus, Popal notes, flip phones are less pricey than book-style options, and Apple is marketing the Duo as one of its most premium products.
Ultimately, the iPhone Duo is just that: a premium option amid a lineup of Apple devices that cater to whatever you need: baseline features with the iPhone 17 , a lighter and thinner handset with the iPhone Air or a more affordable pick with the iPhone 17E . And for photographers who are deterred by the Duo’s lack of a telephoto camera, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will gladly help you part with your money.
“At the very beginning, Samsung positioned the Fold as the best, as the future of smartphones, and that’s not what Apple is doing at all,” Milanesi says. Rather, from the start, the Duo “is an option.”
For those who are enamored but don’t want to fork over nearly two grand upfront, carrier trade-ins and Apple’s Upgrade leasing program could sweeten the deal.

articles.title_zh: Jane Doe in Cornell University case told campus police, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," transcript shows
articles.content_orig:
We're getting new insight into how Cornell University Police handled the case of an alleged fraternity gang rape back in 2024.
Cornell conducted an internal investigation that led to expulsions, suspensions and other sanctions. The response by law enforcement has come under new scrutiny, and prosecutors have now reopened their criminal investigation .
CBS News New York investigative reporter Mahsa Saeidi exclusively obtained a transcript of the alleged victim's interview with campus police from a source.
The interview began on Nov. 14 — more than three weeks after the alleged gang rape — and continued the next day.
A campus police investigator led the questioning. A Title IX investigator, a victim advocate, and Jane Doe's adviser were also in the room for the first day of the interview.
According to the transcript, Jane Doe described drinking and using drugs the night of the alleged rape, and said she had gaps in her memory.
The transcript shows she distinguished the initial sexual activity from what she says happened later, and when asked whether she was OK with the initial encounter, she said, "Yeah, as much as I can be because, again, I was super drunk when I got there ... But I was pretty OK with all of this."
Jane Doe added, according to the transcript, "And then, of course, I was being hit at the same time. Physically hit very, very hard."
According to the transcript, she said she didn't remember the end of the night "where I was raped" and didn't know how many people had sex with her.
When describing what happened later in the night, the transcript says Jane Doe said, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."
The transcript shows that throughout the interview, the investigator asks questions as he prepares her written statement.
Before discussing what Jane Doe said when men asked her for sex, the transcript says the investigator warned her that his questions may sound accusatory, but said he needed specific answers to determine the right charges.
According to the transcript, Jane Doe said she swatted one man's hand away and told him she was uncomfortable, and she told another man no a few times or that she was too tired.
"Was it 'no' or was it, 'eh, I'm tired'?" the investigator asked, according to the transcript.
The transcript says Jane Doe responded, "I think it's 'I'm tired.'"
According to the transcript, the investigator later asked whether she got tired of answering the men's questions and gave in.
"Yes. It was coercion, yes," Jane Doe said, according to the transcript. She also said she was "completely and totally incapacitated."
The transcript shows the investigator documenting her account, reading it back and asking her to clarify or correct it.
On the second day of the interview, Jane Doe reviewed the revised six-page statement. The transcript shows her adviser asked if she wanted her and another adviser to review the statement.
Before signing, the transcript shows Jane Doe said, "I'm very confident about this."
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten says his decision not to bring charges was based on the contents of Jane Doe's signed 2024 statement.
But he told CBS News New York's Saeidi on Tuesday that he had never seen the transcript showing what Jane Doe told campus police before his office decided not to bring charges.
"I'm going to follow up on this because this is news to me," he said.
When told Jane Doe had said she was confident she was raped, Van Houten said, "That wasn't information that I had, first of all. Second of all, that is a legal conclusion."
"If she had said those words, we certainly would want to have explored that more," Van Houten continued. "Like I said, that wasn't provided to me."
The DA said he'd seek the transcript and follow up with Cornell Police.
"Nobody knows this information about the transcript and that gives me something to really dig into because that changes the landscape for me," Van Houten said.
Cornell University said its police department provided the results of the school's investigation to the DA.
Jane Doe's attorney, Thomas Giuffra, remarked to CBS News, "What more did (Van Houten) need to do a thorough investigation and prosecute? He had a woman who told an officer she was raped and a group chat inviting sexual assaults . The failure to do anything is shocking.
"Neither I nor Ms. Doe have any confidence in DA Houten's ability to handle this investigation and prosecution. He seems more interested in protecting his reputation as opposed to seeking justice as is his duty as the District Attorney."
Previously, Giuffra said his client was in denial after the alleged attack.
CBS News New York has not seen Jane Doe's final six-page statement. CBS News New York reached out to Cornell but and has not heard back.
